﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ The discussion of the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah has already passed, as has the discussion of their counterpart in Surat Yunus.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, that you might bring mankind out of darknesses into light, by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ The discussion of the construction ﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. A Book We have sent down to you﴾ is like the discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1] and ﴿A Book We have sent down to you﴾. Apart from this verse, in which the agent of the sending down is mentioned, and which is known from the root *inzal* (sending down), indicating that it comes from the higher world. Thus, since it is known, the omission of the agent in the verse of Surat al-A'raf is equivalent to it. This omission is what the apparent sense and brevity require. But here He mentions it because the context is one of bestowing favour upon people, which is derived from the causal clause ﴿that you might bring mankind out of darknesses into light﴾, and from the mention of the attribute of lordship in ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾. This differs from the verse of Surat al-A'raf, which is in a context of reassurance and steadfastness for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to whom the Book was sent down. So mentioning the one to whom it was sent down, and restricting the statement to him, was more important in that context, together with what it contains of fulfilling the right of brevity.

As for the mention of the one to whom it was sent down here, it is to honour his status, and so that he may have a share in this favour, which is the share of intermediation, as His saying ﴿that you might bring mankind out of darknesses into light﴾ indicates. It also causes distress to the obstinate and to those who hate the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

For this purpose, the attributes of the agent of the sending down are stated explicitly three times in ﴿by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy﴾, after the context had called for a pronoun, in keeping with ﴿We have sent it down﴾.

The attribution of the bringing out to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is because he conveys this Book, which contains the clarification of the ways of guidance to faith and the exposure of the corruption of polytheism and disbelief. Along with conveying it, he explains it to people and brings its meanings near to them by interpreting and clarifying it, and then by what he builds upon it of admonitions, warnings and glad tidings. Since the bringing out has been attributed to him in the context of giving the reason for sending the Book down to him, it is known that his bringing them out of darknesses is through this Book that was sent down, that is, through what it contains of the meanings of guidance.

The giving of the reason for the sending down as bringing out of darknesses shows that guidance is what God, exalted is He, desires from people, and that He has not left them in their misguidance. Whoever is guided is guided by God's direction, and whoever goes astray does so by preferring error and caprice over the signs of guidance. The command of God is only for wise purposes and benefits, some of which are greater than others.

*Al-ikhraj* (bringing out) is used figuratively for moving from one state to another. The transition is likened to going out, and so the conveyance is called bringing out.

*Al-zulumat* (darknesses) and *al-nur* (light) are metaphors for disbelief and faith. Disbelief places its bearer in bewilderment, so it is like darkness in that respect, while faith guides to the truth, so it is like light in clarifying the way. The listener may derive from this an image of the one immersed in disbelief as one bewildered in darkness, and of his transition to faith as the state of one who comes out of darkness into a bright place.

The plural *al-zulumat* and the singular *al-nur* were discussed at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

The *ba'* in ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ indicates cause. *Al-idhn* (permission) is a command to do an act that depends on the consent of the one who commands it, and it is God's command to Him to send him to them. This is the permission that pertains to all people, as in His saying ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of God﴾ [al-Nisa: 64]. Since the sending was for their benefit, the permission was attributed to the attribute of the Lord, joined to the pronoun for people, that is, by the permission of the One who manages their interests.

His saying ﴿to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ is an apposition (badal) to *al-nur*, with the preposition repeated for the substituted noun, to add clarification to the thing replaced and to give it emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The chiefs of those among his people who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75] in Surat al-A'raf. The suitability of the path, used figuratively for the true religion, to the figurative bringing out, darknesses and light, and to what it includes of imagery, is evident.

The choice of the attributes ﴿the Almighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ from among the lofty attributes is for their greater suitability to the context, since "the Almighty" is the One who cannot be overcome. The sending down of the Book is a proof of the truth of what God desires from people, so He prevails over the opponents and establishes the proof against them.

*Al-Hamid* (the Praiseworthy) means *al-mahmud* (the One who is praised), because the sending down of this Book is a great blessing that guides to praising Him for it. By this, the two attributes encompass the indication of both groups: whoever is inclined to guidance from the first moment, and whoever argues and then comes to guidance after the establishment of the proof and the exhaustion of his stratagems.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 2–3:

﴿Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read the name Allah in the nominative (raf'), as a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), the implied sense being: "He (i.e., the Mighty, the Praiseworthy) is Allah, the One described as the One to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." This omission is in accordance with the omission of the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) in the view of the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani), following al-Sakkaki, for the sake of following usage (mutaba'at al-isti'mal), that is, the usage of the Arabs: when a thing described by attributes is mentioned, they move from that to reporting about it something greater than what has been mentioned, so that this transition gains an emphasis on the purpose. Like the saying of Ibrahim al-Suli:

I shall thank 'Amr if my death is delayed, for favours he has not reproached me for, however great they are,

a youth whose wealth is not hidden from his friend, and who does not display complaint when the sandal slips.

That is: he is a youth whose attributes are such-and-such.

The rest of the readers, except Ruwais from Ya'qub, read it in the genitive (jarr) as an apposition (badaliyyah) to "the Mighty, the Praiseworthy" [Ibrahim: 1]. This is an Arabic method, and the outcome of the two readings is one; both methods convey that the item introduced by the independent statement is more worthy of mention after what preceded it, since the name Allah is greater than the rest of the attributes, for it is the proper name of the Essence, which no existent shares in its absoluteness, nor in its original meaning from which it was transferred to being a proper name. However, the nominative is stronger and more majestic.

Ruwais from Ya'qub read it in the nominative when pausing at His saying "the Praiseworthy" and beginning with the name "Allah"; but when "the Praiseworthy" is connected with the name "Allah," the name Allah is read in the genitive as an apposition.

The describing of Allah by the relative clause is for the increase of magnificence, not for definition; since sovereignty over all existents is a great attribute, and Allah is known by it among the addressees. In it is an implicit allusion (ta'rid) that the path of other than Allah, the ways of their gods, does not lead to the intended goal, because of the deficiency of those who possess it. And in mentioning this relative clause is an incidental allusion (idmaj ta'rid) against the polytheists who worshipped that which the heavens and the earth do not belong to.

﴿And woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment, those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter, and bar from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked. Those are in far error.﴾

When His saying "to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy" [Ibrahim: 1], and "Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," conveyed an implicit allusion against the polytheists who followed the path of other than Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, the discourse turned to threatening and warning them with His saying "And woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment." That is: to those who associate other gods with Him.

The sentence "And woe to the disbelievers" is a performative (insha') supplication against them in a context of anger and blame, like their saying "Woe to you" (wayhaka); so its conjunction is a conjunction of performative to declarative.

"Woe" (wayl) is a verbal noun for which no verb is known. Its meaning is destruction and what approaches it of evil condition. Because no verb is known for it, it is an ism masdar and is treated as verbal nouns: it is put in the accusative as an absolute object, and it is put in the nominative to convey permanence, as already mentioned in the nominative of "al-hamdu lillah" in Surat al-Fatihah. It is said: "Woe to you" and "Woe to you" with the possessive suffix; and it is said: "Ya waylaka," with the vocative. Sometimes after this construction its cause is mentioned, and it is brought in the genitive with the preposition min (of origin), as in His saying here "because of a severe punishment," meaning: destruction that befalls them from the severe punishment they encounter, which is the punishment of the Fire. Woe was previously mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, "So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands" [al-Baqarah: 79] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The disbelievers here are the known ones, those who did not come out of the darknesses into the light, nor followed the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, nor benefited from the Book which was sent down to bring them out of the darknesses into the light.

صفحة ١٨٤
"Yastahibbuna" means "yuhibbuna" (they love); the sin and ta' are for emphasis, like (istaqdama) and (ista'khara). "Yastahibbuna" was made to imply the meaning of "yu'thiruna" (they prefer), because love reached "the worldly life" after mention of the severe punishment for them; this indicated that they love the good of this world without the good of the Hereafter, since in the Hereafter they are in misery. From this arose the meaning of preference, so it was made to imply it, and so it took another object by means of the preposition "'ala" (over) in His saying "'ala al-akhirah," that is: they prefer it over it.

His saying "wa yasuddunna 'an sabil Allah wa yabghunaha 'iwajan" has a parallel previously mentioned in His saying: "Verily the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers who bar from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked" [al-A'raf: 44] in Surat al-A'raf, and at His saying, exalted is He, "O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses?" [Al 'Imran: 99] in Surat Al 'Imran; so refer to it there.

Barring from the way of Allah is preventing those who would enter Islam from entering it. This is likened to one who prevents a passerby from traversing the road; and the road is called the way of Allah because it leads to His pleasure, so it is as if it leads to Him. Or it means they bar themselves from the way of Allah, because they neglected their faculties and perceptions of reflecting upon the verses of the Qur'an; so it is as if they have barred them from walking in the way of Allah, and they seek the crooked path. Thus it is known that the way of Allah is straight, as He said: "And that this is My path, straight, so follow it" [al-An'am: 153].

The demonstrative in His saying "those are in far error" is to alert that they deserve what has been described of error, because of their barring from the way of truth and their seeking the way of falsehood. So "ula'ika" is in the place of a subject (mubtada'), and "fi dalalin ba'id" is its predicate; and the particle of location indicates that error encompasses them, so they are firmly established in it.

Describing error as "far" may be a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), the far ones being really the astray themselves, meaning: an error by which they went far from the truth, so the farness was attributed to its cause.

It is also possible that the intended description by farness is by likening it to a vast road from which the traveler's return is difficult, meaning: a strong error from which its owner finds it hard to desist. In it is a sense of remoteness regarding the guidance of such people, like His saying: "Surely those who dispute concerning the Hour are in far error" [al-Shura: 18], and His saying: "Nay, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error" [Saba': 8]. And it has been mentioned at His saying: "And whoever associates partners with Allah has indeed strayed far astray" [al-Nisa': 116] in Surat al-Nisa'.

If the form of restriction (al-qasr) is used in its apparent sense and applies to the related elements of the restricted verb, it is a relative restriction (qasr idafi) aimed at correcting the belief of the addressees. It must therefore be a rebuttal of a group of the polytheists who said: "Why was the Qur'an not revealed in the language of non-Arabs (al-'ajam)?" Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Kashshaf, at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Had We made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said: "Why have its verses not been explained in detail? What, a non-Arabic book for an Arab people?"﴾ [Fussilat: 44], that they were saying, out of their obstinacy: "Why was the Qur'an not revealed in the language of non-Arabs?" It is also narrated in al-Tabari's Tafsir at that place, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that the Arabs said this.

Then it is permissible that what is meant by "the language of non-Arabs" is the language of others than the Arabs, such as Hebrew (al-'Ibraniyyah) or Syriac (al-Suryaniyyah), among the languages in which the Torah and the Gospel were revealed. Among the things their illusions had made appear to them was that they supposed the divine books have a special language in which they are revealed and then explained to those who do not know that language. This is a widespread belief among people of weak minds. Those who deal with the secret of letters and talismans (al-talsamat) claim that these can be acquired only through the Syriac language, and they assert that it is the language of the angels and the language of the spirits. Al-Siraj al-Bulqini claimed that the questioning in the grave takes place in the Syriac language, and Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti received this from him, found it strange, and said:

"Among the most astonishing things the two eyes have seen is that the questioning of the grave is in Syriac; our shaykh al-Bulqini issued this ruling, and I have not seen it from anyone else with my own eyes."

[Page 186]

Some Arabs who had become Christians, and some of them who had become Jews, such as the Arabs of Yemen, had parts of the Torah and the Gospel translated for them into Arabic, as occurred in the hadith of Waraqah ibn Nawfal in the Book of the Beginning of Revelation in Sahih al-Bukhari. Thus there became established in the souls of the polytheists, among their criticisms, that if the Qur'an were from God, it would be in the language in which the earlier books had come. So its Arabic character became for them one of the aspects of their criticism that it was sent down from God. Therefore the restriction here is to refute their statement, meaning: We did not send any messenger with a tongue other than the tongue of his own people to whom he was sent, not with the tongue of other peoples.

The placement of this verse after the verse ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you﴾ [Ibrahim: 1] has clear relevance.

The construction of the text is estimated as: "A Book which We have sent down to you, that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light," and We sent it down in the language of your people, that you may make clear to them what We have revealed to you. And We did not send any messenger except with the tongue of his people, that he might make clear to them, so that He would bring them out of darkness into light.

If the form of restriction is employed contrary to what the apparent meaning requires, and it is not a reply to the statement of some of the polytheists, then it is a treatment of the polytheists as if they were not Arabs, because they were not affected by the verses of the Qur'an, and because of their saying: ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. The basis of the restriction is what follows the particle of cause (lam al-'illah). The meaning is: We did not send you except that you might make clear to them, and We did not send any messenger except that he might make clear to his people. His saying ﴿except with the tongue of his people﴾ is an inclusion (idmaj) within the exception upon which the restriction is applied. Or it may be linked to the verb "that he might make clear," placed before it. The estimate is: We did not send you except that you might make clear to them in their tongue, and We did not send any messenger except that he might make clear to his people in their tongue. So why has your people not been guided by this Qur'an, when it is in their tongue? With this, the connection of the consequence in His saying ﴿So God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ becomes clear.

Al-lisan (tongue) means language and that by which communication takes place. It is applied to language by the figure of speech in which the name of the locus is used for what inheres in it, like "the valley flowed." The letter ba' (bi) denotes association, so the language of his people is associated with his speech and with the Book revealed to him for guiding them.

[Page 187]

Al-qawm (people) means a nation and a group. The people of each person are his kinsmen whose group is one and who speak one language. The people of each messenger are his community to whom he was sent, since messengers were sent to their peoples. The people of Muhammad ﷺ are the Arabs. As for his community (ummah), they are the peoples to whom he was sent, and they are all of mankind.

The first addressees were the Arabs among whom he lived, and the Book was revealed in their language, because it was impossible for it to be revealed in the languages of all nations. So God chose that His Messenger ﷺ should be from a nation that is the most eloquent of nations in speech, the swiftest in understanding, the most intelligent, and the best prepared to accept guidance and direction. No group of people believed in any messenger during his lifetime as many as those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ during his lifetime. Islam spread throughout the lands of the Arabs, and about fifty thousand or more performed the Pilgrimage with the Prophet ﷺ at the Farewell Pilgrimage. It is said: one hundred thousand, being the men who were able to perform it.

He chose that the Book revealed to them should be in the language of the Arabs, because it is the most suitable of languages for gathering meanings, for conciseness of expression, for ease of flow on the tongues, for speed of memorization, and for beauty of effect on the ears. The Arab nation was made the first to receive the Book, and it was entrusted with spreading it among the nations.

In the ta'lil (giving of cause) by His saying ﴿that he might make clear to them﴾ there is an indication of this meaning. Because the purpose of the legislation is clarification, the languages closest to clarification among the languages of the nations to which he was sent is the language that is most worthy for the Book to come in. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in plain Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193–195]. All of this is within the implications (matawi) of this verse.

However, since the purpose of its context is to refute their criticism that it was revealed in a language in which no earlier book had been revealed, the verse limited itself, in rebutting their error, to saying that it was only like this so that it might make clear to them, because that is what concerns them.

[Page 188]

The consequence of His saying ﴿So God leads astray whom He wills﴾, etc., is based on the whole sentence ﴿We did not send any messenger except with the tongue of his people, that he might make clear to them﴾. For this reason the verb "yudill" (leads astray) came in the nominative and not the subjunctive, since it is not coordinated with the verb "liyubayyina" (that he might make clear). This is because leading astray is not caused by clarification. Rather, it is a consequence of the sending, which is caused by clarification. The meaning is that sending in the tongue of his people is for the wisdom of clarification, and the effect of clarification may be achieved through the aid of guidance, and it may not be achieved because of the misguidance of those to whom it is made clear. Misguidance and guidance come from God, through what He has placed in people's souls of differing readiness.

The clause ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is a conclusion (tadhyil), because al-'Aziz (the Mighty) is strong, so that nothing escapes His power and nothing goes outside what He created it for; and al-Hakim (the Wise) places things in their proper places. So the position of sending and clarification comes in the most perfect form of guidance, and the position of misguidance and guidance is the creation proceeding in the most suitable condition in accordance with the circumstances of those to whom he was sent. Thus clarification is required by the command of legislation, and misguidance is required by the command of creation.

[Page 189]

Since the preceding verses were directed at those who denied that the Qur'an was sent down from God, He followed this rebuttal with an analogy (tamthil) based on a parallel case: the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) to his people with a message like the one Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent with, and for the same purpose that Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, namely to bring his people out of darkness into light.

The emphasis on the report of Musa's (peace be upon him) sending, through the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq), places the deniers' rejection of Muhammad's (ﷺ) message in the position of one who denies the message of Musa (peace be upon him). Their denial of Muhammad's (ﷺ) message calls for this placement, because what is valid for the like is valid for the like-in-kind. Moreover, some of them said ﴿God has not sent down anything to any human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. The preposition (ba') in "bi-ayatina" indicates accompaniment (lil-musahabah), meaning: a sending accompanied by signs that demonstrate the truth of his mission, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent accompanied by the sign of the Qur'an, which demonstrates that it is from God. Thus the analogy is complete, and the proof stands against the deniers. The word "an" (that) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), explaining the sending by the clause ﴿bring out your people﴾, and the sending contains the sense of speech, so it is fitting for the explanatory "an" to be used.

"Al-zulumat" (the darknesses) is used metaphorically (musta'ar) for polytheism and sins, and "al-nur" (the light) is used metaphorically for true faith and God-consciousness (taqwa). This is because when the period became long for the Children of Israel in Egypt after the death of Yusuf (peace be upon him), polytheism crept into them and they followed the religion of the Copts. Therefore the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) was to correct their beliefs, alongside calling Pharaoh and his people to faith in the One God. It ultimately aimed at bringing the Children of Israel out of polytheism and corruption and admitting them into the enclosure of faith and righteousness.

"Al-tadhkir" (reminding) is the removal of forgetfulness of something. It is also used for teaching something unknown whose nature was that it should be known. Since "al-tadhkir" was here given the sense of warning and admonition (infar and wa'z), it takes the preposition "bi-", meaning: remind them with a reminder that admonishes, through the Days of God.

The ﴿Days of God﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] are the days on which His might and His overpowering of those who disobeyed His command became manifest, and His support of the believers against their enemy. All of this is a manifestation of the might of God, exalted is He. It has become common to use the name "day" in construct with the name of a person or tribe to refer to a day on which the bearer of the name prevailed over his enemy; it is said, "the days of Tamim," meaning the days of their victory. Thus the "Days of God" are the days on which His power became manifest, when He destroyed those who disbelieved in Him, and when He granted victory to His allies and to those who obeyed Him.

[Page 190]

So what is meant by ﴿the Days of God﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] here are the days on which God delivered the Children of Israel from their enemies, gave them victory, made available to them the means of success and triumph, and showered blessings upon them in the time of Musa (peace be upon him). All of this is among the things Musa (peace be upon him) was commanded to remind them of. All of it may serve as an explanation of the content of the sending, because the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) extended over a period of time, and whenever God revealed to him a reminder during his lifetime, it is part of the content of the mission he brought, and so it is included in the explanation of the sending. Thus the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿O my people, remember the favour of God upon you, when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds. O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20] are part of the reminding by which the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) is explained. Even though this occurred forty years after the beginning of his mission, it was nonetheless a reminder issued during the time of his mission. It is a reminder of the Days of God's great blessings that He gave them, which they would not have obtained had it not been for God's victory for them and His care for them, so that they would know that a weak one may overcome a strong one, and be saved by his weakness, when one of similar strength would not have been saved in his own strength.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the bringing out and the reminding. Thus the bringing out from darkness, after they had sunk deep into it and long periods of time had passed over them in it, is a sign of the power of God, exalted is He. Likewise, reminding them of the Days of God includes signs of God's power and His might and of the support of those who obeyed Him. All of that consists of signs present in the bringing out and in the reminding, in their various states.

The meaning of this comprehensiveness is encompassed by the adverbial particle (harf al-zarfiyyah) in His words ﴿in that﴾, because the notion of containment (zarfiyyah) gathers together different things contained within the container. For this reason the particle of containment has an eloquent placement here. And because the signs are different, some of them being signs of admonition and warning and others signs of favour and encouragement, the phrase was made to relate to ﴿every steadfast, grateful [person]﴾, since steadfastness (sabr) suits warning, because fear of consequences moves the soul to bear opposition to its desires, lest it fall into evil outcomes; and bounty moves the soul to gratitude. Thus the mention of the two qualities was a distribution of what the mention of the Days of God had summarized, namely days of hardship and days of blessing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 6:

﴿And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "Remember the favor of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord."﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾ [Ibrahim: 5], in terms of the purpose of the two clauses, which is to draw a parallel with the customs of what the earlier messengers brought in guiding and admonishing their nations, just as the Qur'an was revealed for that purpose.

"Idh" (when) is an adverbial of time (zarf) referring to the past, and it is connected to a verb whose implied form is "udhkur" (remember). The context indicates this, which is the mention of historical examples concerning the circumstances of the messengers, peace be upon them, with their nations. The meaning is: and remember the statement of Moses to his people, etc.

This is among what Moses said to his people after Allah had saved them from the subjugation and humiliation of the Copts. It is thus a detailed account of what was meant by the sending of Moses, peace be upon him. It is part of the reminder of the "days of Allah," which Allah commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to remind his people of.

"Idh najjakum" (when He saved you) is an adverbial of time (zarf) for "the favor" in the sense of "bounty." That is, the bounty that occurred at the time of His saving you from the people of Pharaoh. The explanation of its parallel was already given in His saying, ﴿And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 141], in Surat al-Baqarah, and likewise in Surat al-Aʿraf (where it says "they kill"). The only difference is that in this verse the clause "and they slaughter" (wa yudhabbihuna) is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause "they inflict" (yasumunakum). In the verses of al-Baqarah and al-Aʿraf, the clause "they slaughter" (yudhabbihuna) and the clause "they kill" (yaqtulun) are used without conjunction, on the basis that they are an inclusive apposition (badal ishtimal) of the clause ﴿they inflict the worst torment﴾.

[Page 192]

Thus the content of the clause "and they slaughter" here is intended to be counted separately, as if it were a category other than "the worst torment," out of concern for its gravity. Its conjunction is therefore a conjunction of the particular to the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm). Under both arrangements, attention has been given to this particular torment mentioned explicitly. The Qur'an conveyed the intended meaning of Moses's statement, peace be upon him, by mentioning the more general torment and then the more specific, for the sake of emphasis. This is achieved in both arrangements. The Qur'an narrated it in each place in a different manner, as a variation in retelling the story, with a difference in the form of the wording while preserving the meaning conveyed, which is the mention of the worst torment in general terms and the mention of its most atrocious kinds in detail.

As for the conjunction of the clause ﴿and they keep your women alive﴾ in the three verses, this is because its content, taken on its own, is not suitable for explaining "the worst torment," since keeping women alive is in itself a favor. However, it becomes part of the torment when it is joined with the slaughter of the sons, for it is known that their purpose in keeping the women alive was to enslave them and humiliate them. Thus keeping them alive, with that intent, became a preparation for their torment. For this reason, all of that was called a trial (balaʾ).

The root meaning of "balaʾ" is "testing." Here, "balaʾ" means a calamity of evil. It was named by the term for testing because it is a test of the measure of patience. Thus "balaʾ" is used here for severe hardship, by naming a thing after what it leads to, in the manner of metonymy (majaz mursal). This usage has become so common in the form of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) that it is hardly used except for what is disliked. What is used in the sense of good comes only in the form of the verb, such as His saying, ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya: 35], and His saying, ﴿and We will test your reports﴾ [Muhammad: 31]. This was already discussed in its parallel in Surat al-Baqarah.

This harm which befell them is attributed to Allah because His abandonment of the people of Pharaoh to do such things, and His not showing kindness to the Children of Israel, makes it as if it came from Allah. It is a punishment for the Children of Israel's abandonment of their true religion, which Abraham had enjoined upon his sons and Jacob, peace be upon them, and their following the religion of the Copts and worship of their gods. The choice of the description "Lord" (Rabb) here is to hint that He intended by it the good of their future and to alert them to avoid worshipping idols and distorting the religion, like His saying, ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Isra: 8].

[Page 193]

This verse includes what is in verse 17 of chapter 21, and verse 3 of chapter 13 of the Book of Exodus, and what is in verse 13 of chapter 26 of the Book of Leviticus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 7:

﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe."﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿when He delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [Ibrahim: 6]. Thus it is part of the speech of Musa (peace be upon him), and the implied meaning is: "Remember the favor of Allah upon you, when your Lord proclaimed: 'If you are grateful...'" etc. This is because the reward for thankfulness for a favor with an increase from it is itself a favor and a bounty from Allah, since gratitude to the Benefactor is obligatory, and so one would not deserve a reward were it not for the vastness of Allah's bounty. As for His saying ﴿but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾, it was brought by way of contrast (muqabalah).

It is also permissible to conjoin ﴿and when your Lord proclaimed﴾ to ﴿the favor of Allah upon you﴾ [Ibrahim: 6], in which case the implied meaning is: "Remember when your Lord proclaimed," with (idh) being in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bih) and not as an adverb of time; this is one of its usages. It has already been discussed under His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-A'raf ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them﴾ [al-A'raf: 167], and His saying ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-A'raf: 86].

The meaning of ﴿your Lord proclaimed﴾ is: He spoke a clear speech, i.e., He addressed Musa (peace be upon him) with what this verse contains, in the hearing of the community of the Children of Israel. Perhaps this speech is what is found in paragraphs 9 and 20 of chapter 9 of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj), and paragraphs 1, 18 and 22 of chapter 20 of it, and paragraphs 20 to 30 of chapter 23 of it.

Ta'adhdhun (proclamation) is an intensification of adhan (announcement); one says adhdhana and ta'adhdhana just as one says tawa'ada and awada (to threaten), and tafaddala and afdala (to favor). Thus the pattern taffaʿala carries an added meaning over the pattern afʿala.

The clause ﴿If you are grateful﴾ serves as a preface (muwattiʾah) to an oath, and the oath is used for emphasis. Gratitude implies a favor, so what is meant is gratitude for the favor of deliverance from the people of Pharaoh and other favors. For this reason the object of ﴿you are grateful﴾ and the object of ﴿I will surely increase you﴾ are omitted, so that they are understood generally for both verbs.

Page 194
Kufr (ungratefulness) here means ungratefulness for favors, which is confronting the Benefactor with disobedience. The greatest kufr is denying the Creator or worshipping other than Him alongside Him, which is shirk, just as gratitude is confronting the favor by manifesting servitude and obedience.

By ﴿indeed My punishment is severe﴾ He dispensed with (La-u'adhdhibannakum ʿadhaban shadidan, "I will surely punish you with a severe punishment"), because it is more general and more concise, and because conveying the threat by a kind of allusion (taʿrid) has a greater effect on the soul. The meaning is: "Indeed My punishment is severe for whoever disbelieves," so you, in that case, would be among them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 8:

﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on the earth all together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ The verb of saying (qawl) is repeated in the coordination of one part of Moses' speech (peace be upon him) upon another, lest it be supposed that this is something the Lord had permitted to be said, and it is rather an alert to the speech of Allah. In the repetition of the verb of saying there is emphasis on this sentence and highlighting of it, so that it stands out on its own and so that those listening to the Qur'an attend to it.

The aspect of its importance is that most disbelievers reckon that they do good to Allah by their faith, and that their prophets, when they insist upon them to believe, only seek by that to strengthen their own side and to be eager for their benefit. So when He promised them increase for thankfulness and threatened them with punishment for disbelief, He feared they might reckon that this was out of the vindictiveness of the one who rewards, by what He rewarded, and the harm to Him from what He punished, so He alerted them to this satanic thought, lest it creep into their souls and thereby earn them conceit in their faith and thankfulness and abandonment of disbelief.

The "antum" (you) is separated between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, since this conjoined-to is an attached pronoun.

Page 195
"Jami'an" (all together) is an emphasis for "man fi al-ard" (whoever is on the earth), for the explicit statement of generality. Its parallel has already been mentioned, and its being in the accusative is not far off.

Al-Ghani (Free of need) is the one who has no need of anything, so there enters into the generality of His freedom from need that He is free of need of those who disbelieve in Him.

Al-Hamid (Praiseworthy) is the one who is praised. The meaning is that He is praiseworthy from you, and independent of your praise. Even if they disbelieved in Him, they would still be praising Him by the tongue of their state, unwillingly, for every blessing that reaches them they praise, and they only praise Allah Most High by it, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. And this verse includes what is in paragraphs 30 to 33 of chapter 32 of the Book of Exodus.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 9:**

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands over their mouths and said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with, and we are truly in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾

This statement is a new, independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a fresh sentence that begins a new topic) in which the address returns to the polytheists of the Arabs, by way of *iltifat* (a shift from one grammatical person to another). In His words "Has there not come to you," the address is directed at the disbelievers, who are the ones meant by His words ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 2], and who are the majority of the people meant by His words ﴿to bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]. After the matter was stated in summary in His words, exalted is He, ﴿We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 4] and what follows it, it was then explained in detail by presenting the sending of messengers to them for the purpose of bringing them out of darkness into light, through the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) to bring out his people. The matter was then completed after this with a comprehensive statement about the conditions of the nations and their messengers. It therefore served as a *hawsala* (a summary that gathers and concludes what has come before), and a *tadhyil* (a concluding addition that restates a general truth), together with a representation of their condition by the condition of the earlier nations, and the similarity of their rational arguments in their false proofs, and the messengers' rejection of them in the same way the Qur'an rejected the polytheists in several places. Then it was closed with a threat.

The interrogative is for denial (*istifham inkari*), because they had already received the reports of these nations. As for the people of Noah, the news of them had spread widely among the nations because of the account of the Flood. As for 'Ad and Thamud, they were Arabs, and their dwellings are in their lands, which they pass by and tell one another about. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾ [Ibrahim: 45], and He said ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 137].

﴿And those after them﴾ includes the people of Madyan, the companions of the Rass, the people of Tubba', and others of nations that became extinct and whose reports vanished, so that none knows them except Allah. This is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass and many generations in between﴾ [al-Furqan: 38].

The clause ﴿whom none knows except Allah﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*mu'taridah*) between ﴿those after them﴾ and the clause ﴿their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, which is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to ﴿those after them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. It is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the great number, which is implied by the absence of people's knowledge of them. The meaning of ﴿their messengers came to them﴾ is that every nation had its messenger come to it.

The pronouns in (*radd*) "they returned," (*aydiyahum*) "their hands," and (*afwahihim*) "their mouths" all refer to the people of Noah and what is joined to them by conjunction.

I do not know of any precedent for this construction in the speech of the Arabs, so it may well be one of the novel expressions of the Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿they put their hands over their mouths﴾ admits of several possibilities. Al-Zamakhshari (in *al-Kashshaf*) pushed them to seven, and some of them are remote. The most evident of them is that the meaning is: they placed their hands over their mouths to hide their intense laughter at the speech of the messengers, out of dislike for their inner mouths being revealed. This is a representation of the state of mockery toward the messengers.

The word *radd* ("return") is used here to mean the repeated placing of hands on the mouths, as al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) pointed out: that is, they placed their hands on their mouths, then removed them, then placed them again, and that repeated placing is a "return."

The particle *fi* ("in") here indicates figurative location, meant to convey firm establishment, and so it is in the sense of *'ala* ("on"), as in His words ﴿Those are in far-off error﴾ [Ibrahim: 3]. Thus the meaning of "they returned their hands in their mouths" is "they placed their hands on their mouths." Its connection with the particle of consequence *fa-* (then) indicates that they hastened to place their hands on their mouths immediately upon receiving the call of their messengers. This implies that placing the hands on the mouths is a representation of the state of one who is amazed and mocking. The expression is therefore a representation of a customary state, and its literal meaning is not intended, because its being reported about the nations, despite the difference of their customs and gestures and the difference of individuals in their movements when amazed, is evidence that it was intended only as an Arabic idiom.

A parallel to this is His words, exalted is He, reporting the people of Paradise: ﴿And they say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has given us the land as an inheritance"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. The inheritance of the land is a metonymy for a good outcome, following the usage of the Arabs when their tribes compete, that a good outcome belongs to whoever seizes the land of his enemy.

They affirmed their disbelief in what the messengers brought by what is indicated by *inna* ("indeed") and by the past-tense verb in their words "We disbelieved." They called what they disbelieved in "sent" (*mursalan*) with mockery toward the messengers, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]. The meaning of this is that they disbelieved that what they brought was sent from Allah; that is, they disbelieved that Allah had sent them. This is among the matters they were certain of in denying it.

As for their words ﴿And we are truly in doubt about that to which you invite us﴾, this is doubt about the soundness and correctness of what the messengers invite them to. In their view it is open to examination and to distinguishing its sound from its unsound. Thus the object of doubt is what the messengers invite them to, while the object of denial is attributing their call to Allah. So their intention is: even if they were lying in claiming prophethood, some of what they call to may still be true and right, for a liar may sometimes say what is true.

They made the doubt strong, so it was expressed as their being enclosed within it, meaning it surrounds them and is firmly established in them to the utmost degree.

The word *murib* ("causing suspicion") is an emphasis on the meaning of "in doubt." *Murib* means one who causes suspicion, and it is a synonym of doubt. So describing doubt as *murib* is an emphasis of its essence, like the expressions *laylun alyal* ("a very dark night") and *sha'irun sha'ir* ("a true poem"). [In Arabic: لَيْلٌ ألْيَلُ، وشِعْرٌ شاعِرٌ.]

One of the two nuns in *inna* ("indeed") in His words *inna* ("we") has been dropped for lightness, to avoid the heaviness that arises from two other nuns coming together after it in *tad'unana* ("you invite us"), both of which must be mentioned. This is unlike the verse in Surah Hud, ﴿And indeed we are in doubt about what you invite us to﴾ [Hud: 62], where *wa-inna-na* ("and indeed we") is written with both nuns, since there was no reason for lightening there, because the addressed person in *tad'una* ("you invite") there is singular.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 10:

﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God, Originator of the heavens and the earth? He invites you that He may forgive you of your sins and reprieve you until a specified term."﴾ It is a rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkari), and the object of the denial is the occurrence of doubt concerning the existence of God. The object of the doubt has therefore been placed first, for the sake of emphasis on it. Had he said, "Do I doubt in God?", it would not have had this impact, like the words of al-Qatami:

Is it disbelief, after the death was turned back from me, and after your gift of a hundred grazing camels?
It would have been more eloquent for him, had he been able to say: "Is it disbelief after the death was turned back from me?"

The name of Majesty (ism al-jalala) is linked to doubt, and a proper noun (al-ism al-'alam) indicates the essence. The intended meaning is the denial that doubt occurs concerning the most important of the divine attributes, which is the attribute of being singled out for divinity, that is, the attribute of unity (wahdaniyya).

The name of Majesty is followed by the descriptive phrase that indicates His existence, namely the existence of the heavens and the earth, which indicates that they have a wise Creator, since such wondrous, orderly created things could not proceed from a non-choosing agent. This is known with minimal reflection, and it is a confirmation of the denial that doubt occurs regarding His being singled out for divinity, because His being singled out for creation necessitates His being singled out for the entitlement to be worshipped by His creatures.

The clause "He invites you" (yad'ukum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the name of Majesty, meaning: He invites you to renounce disbelief, that He may forgive you what you have committed of polytheism, and ward off from you the punishment of annihilation, so that He reprieves you in life until a customary term.

The du'a' (invitation, calling) is essentially a call (nida'). It is figuratively applied to command and guidance, because the commander calls the one commanded.

The verb of invitation is usually followed by the thing invited to with the preposition of termination, which is (ila) "to", as in the words of God, related about the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿And, O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41]. It may also be followed by the preposition of causation (lam al-ta'lil) introducing that which has been made the cause of the invitation, since causation indicates the effect, as in His words: ﴿And indeed, whenever I have called them, that You may forgive them﴾ [Nuh: 7]; that is, I called them to the cause of forgiveness, that You may forgive them, i.e., I called them to faith so that You might forgive them. And it is so in this verse as well: He invites you to monotheism, that He may forgive you your sins.

The verb of invitation may also be followed by the object invited to with the lam, by treating the thing one is invited to reach as if it were the thing for the sake of which one is invited, as in the words of a Bedouin of the Banu Asad:

I called for what befell me, Miswar, so he answered, and the answer was at the hands of Miswar.

* * *

﴿They said: "You are only human beings like us, you wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship. So bring us a clear authority."﴾ They intended to silence the messengers by cutting off the theoretical argument. They denied that the messengers were distinguished by anything additional in their human form by which it could be known that God had chosen them over others by making them His messengers. These peoples supposed that this was a more decisive refutation of the messengers' argument, since the likeness between them and their peoples is perceptible and does not require lengthy argumentation. Therefore they demanded that their messengers bring a perceptible proof establishing that God had chosen them for His message, and they reckoned that this would be a challenge.

The clause "you wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is a qualification of what the restriction in the clause "You are only human beings like us" implies, namely the denial that they are messengers from God with a religion that opposes their ancient religion. On that basis, the clause "So bring us a clear authority" is introduced as a consequence, because the mere fact that they are human does not require demanding that they bring a clear authority; rather, what required it was that they had come to nullify the religion of their people, and this is the content of what they were sent with.

They expressed their religion with the relative form (al-mawsuliyya), because of what the relative clause indicates of exalting their religion as the inheritance of their fathers, whom they consider protected from following falsehood. Nations have a sanctification of their forebears, and therefore they turned away from saying "you wish to turn us away from our religion."

The sultan (sultan) is the proof (hujja), and it has been mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Do you dispute with me about names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority?﴾ [al-A'raf: 71] in Surat al-A'raf.

The mubin (clear) is that which is evident, leaving no possibility of anything other than what it indicates.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 11–12:

Page 201
﴿Their messengers said to them, "We are only humans like you, but Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants. And it was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿And why should we not rely upon Allah while He has guided us to our ways? And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with. And upon Allah let those who rely [upon Him] rely.﴾

The statement of the messengers, ﴿We are only humans like you﴾, is a reply by way of "al-qawl bil-muwajab" (accepting the premise) in the science of the etiquette of debate (adab al-bahth). It is the acceptance of the premise while the categories remain, by clarifying the place of inference, which is not a complete basis for the conclusion; and in it there is an inducement to agreement. Then they turned back against their intended inference with refutation by showing its error. A parallel to this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel therefrom the more humble." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 13:

Page 205
﴿And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, "We will surely drive you out of our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord inspired to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them."﴾ [Ibrahim: 14]

The change of the style of narration to the use of the explicit noun instead of the pronoun indicates that what is meant by "those who disbelieved" here is other than the disbelievers whose narration preceded it, for the narration about them was by way of the pronoun. Thus, the apparent meaning in my view is that what is meant by "those who disbelieved" here is the disbelievers of Quraysh, by way of indirect address (al-tawjih), and that what is meant by "their messengers" is the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), the plural form being applied to his description in the manner of His saying ﴿Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers, they will come to know﴾ [Ghafir: 70] in Surat Ghafir, where what is meant is the polytheists of Mecca, as required by His saying ﴿they will come to know﴾ [Ghafir: 70] and His saying ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences﴾ [al-Hadid: 25] up to His saying ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for the people, and so that Allah may make evident who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]; for what is meant by "the messengers" in the last two passages is the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is the messenger with whom the iron was sent down, i.e., fighting with the sword against the denying people of the call. The use of the plural form for the singular is a metaphor (majaz): either it is a metaphor (isti'arah) if it involves considering the singular as resembling the plural in order to magnify him, as in His saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, return me"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]; or it is a sent metaphor (majaz mursal) if the intention of concealment (al-ta'miyah) is taken into account, its relation then being generality and specificity, and the deviation from the literal meaning toward it being for the purpose of concealment.

Therefore it is certain that what is meant by "those who disbelieved" here is the disbelievers of Mecca, and this is supported by His saying after that ﴿And We will surely settle you in the land after them﴾ [Ibrahim: 14], for it is not known that any messenger from among the messengers of the earlier nations entered the land of his deniers after their destruction and took possession of it except the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). He said during the Farewell Pilgrimage, "Our resting place, God willing, tomorrow is at al-Khayf, the Khayf of the Banu Kinanah, where they swore together upon disbelief."

Page 206

The emphasis of their threat of expulsion by the lam of oath and the nun of emphasis is an expression of eagerness for evil.

And (aw) is for one of two things; they swore to the occurrence of one of the two matters without doubt, one of them from the action of the swearers and the other from the action of the one addressed by the oath. And it is not the (aw) that means (ila) or means (illa).

Al-'awd: returning to something after separation from it. None of the messengers had been following the religion of disbelief, but rather they were withdrawn from the polytheists without any change upon them. So the polytheists thought them to be in agreement with them, and the messengers avoided their gatherings without being aware of their separation from them. When they came to them with the truth, they thought they had moved from agreement with them to opposition to them, so they demanded of them that they return to what they had thought them to be upon.

The locative sense in His saying "in our religion" is figurative, used to mean being able to be engaged in the thing abandoned, as if he had returned to it.

Al-millah: the religion. It was mentioned previously at His saying ﴿a upright religion, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-An'am: 161] at the end of Surat al-An'am, and see His saying ﴿so follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95] at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

Page 207
The clause ﴿So their Lord inspired to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers"﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of the saying of those who disbelieved to their messengers ﴿We will surely drive you out of our land﴾, etc., a consequence of what the saying of those who disbelieved requires of the resolve to expel the messengers from the land; that is, God inspired to the messengers that which strengthens their hearts, namely the promise of destroying the wrongdoers.
The clause ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause "inspired".

The settling of the land: empowering them over it and granting them authority over it, like His saying ﴿and made you inheritors of their land and their homes﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27].

The address in "We will surely settle you" is to the messengers and those who believed in them, so it does not require that the messenger himself dwell in the land of his enemy; it suffices that he have authority over it and that the believers dwell in it, just as God established for His Messenger Mecca and the land of the Hijaz and settled in them those who believed after its conquest.

That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat.

"That" is a demonstrative referring to what was mentioned: the destruction and the settling (of the believers in the land), which were derived from "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers" and "We will surely settle you in the land." The demonstrative is given in the singular, in accordance with the interpretation of "what was mentioned," as in His saying: ﴿And whoever does that will meet with sins﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

The lam (ل) here denotes possession (al-milk), meaning: that is a bestowal and a granting of ownership to whoever fears My standing. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8]. The meaning is: that promise is for whoever fears My standing, that is, it is for you, because you feared My standing. The discourse shifted from the address (second person pronoun) to "whoever fears My standing," because the relative construction indicates that the relative clause is the cause of obtaining that gift.

The meaning of ﴿fears My standing﴾ is "fears Me." The word "standing" (maqam) is inserted for emphasis in the connection of the verb to its object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. This is because maqam originally means the place of standing, and by standing is meant, in a general sense, existence, since things are regarded as standing. So when it is said "fears My standing," there is in it an emphasis that is not in "fears Me": the fear is attached to the place of the one feared. It is said: "he fell short in my regard" (qassara fi janibi), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for what I neglected concerning God's side﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. All of this is a metonymy for the thing it is added to, as in the verse of Ziyad al-A'jam:

"Indeed, generosity, manliness and liberality are in a dome raised over the son of al-Hashraj"

that is, in the son of al-Hashraj, without regard to the existence of an actual dome. And from it is what is in the hadith: "When God created the womb (rahim), it seized the leg of the Throne and said: 'This is the standing of one who seeks refuge in You from severing (ties),'" that is, "this is one who seeks refuge in You from severing."

The fear of God is the fear of His wrath, because the wrath of God is something disliked by His servants.

The clause ﴿and fears My threat﴾ is conjoined to ﴿fears My standing﴾ with the repetition of the verb "fears," rather than conjoining "My threat" to "My standing" alone. This is because, although the literal wording of this relative clause is praise of the addressees, what is intended by it is an allusion to the disbelievers, that they do not fear God's threat. Had it not been for this, the clause ﴿fears My standing﴾ would have sufficed without this clause, for the polytheists did not heed God's threat and regarded it as idle, as He said: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. For this reason He did not combine the two in Surat al-Bayyinah, ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8], because it is in the context of mentioning the bliss of believers specifically.

This verse concerns the mention of the destruction of the wrongdoers and the settling of the believers in their land, so the "standing" was for both groups. Thus in the reward of the believers there is included, by way of incorporation (idmaj), an allusion to the threat against the disbelievers. In combining the two there is an indication that it is incumbent upon the believer to fear the wrath of his Lord and to fear His threat, and those who fear the wrath and threat of God are the pious righteous ones. Thus the meaning of this verse returns to the meaning of the other verse: ﴿that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105].

Al-Jumhur read (wa'idi) without a yā' both in pause and continuation. Warsh, from Nafi', read it without a yā' in pause and with it in continuation. Ya'qub read it with the yā' in both states, continuation and pause. All of this is permissible for the first-person yā' that is attached as a possessive pronoun to a noun, outside of the vocative. In the vocative there are two other dialectal forms.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 15–17:

﴿And they sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed.﴾ ﴿Before him is Hell, and he will be given to drink of festering pus.﴾ ﴿He will gulp it down, but will scarcely be able to swallow it, and death will come to him from every place, yet he will not die; and before him is a harsh torment.﴾

The meaning is that they sought swift victory, and the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَفْتَحُوا﴾ refers to the Messengers. The clause ﴿وَخَابَ كُلُّ جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ﴾ is then coordinated with the clause ﴿فَأَوْحَى إِلَيْهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ﴾ (Ibrahim: 13), etc. That is: so God promised them victory, and those who disbelieved were disappointed, meaning their threat to the Messengers in their words ﴿لَنُخْرِجَنَّكُم مِّنْ أَرْضِنَا أَوْ لَتَعُودُنَّ فِي مِلَّتِنَا﴾ ("We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion", Ibrahim: 13) did not come to pass. The apparent requirement would be to say: "and those who disbelieved were disappointed," but it deviates from this to ﴿كُلُّ جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ﴾ to draw attention to the fact that those who disbelieved were arrogant, stubborn tyrants, and that every arrogant, stubborn tyrant is disappointed. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 18:

Page 212
﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day. They have no power over anything of what they have earned. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ This is an illustration of the state of the good deeds that the polytheists performed, in that they did not benefit from them on the Day of Resurrection. This illustration has raised what the preceding discourse indicated of the severity of their punishment, so there occurs to their minds, or to the minds of whoever among the Muslims hears it, the question of whether they have deeds of kinship and kindness: feeding the poor, freeing slaves, hospitality to guests, bearing the blood-money of others (hamalat diyat), ransoming captives, performing 'umrah, and providing for pilgrims (rifadat al-hajij). Will they find the reward for these? And when the Muslims knew that these do not benefit the disbelievers, their souls sought the way to reconcile the existence of a righteous deed with its failure to benefit when it is needed. So this illustration was struck to explain what resolves all these possibilities.

Al-mathal (the likeness/parable) means the wondrous state. That is, the state of those who disbelieve is wondrous: that their deeds are like ashes, etc. The meaning is: the state of their deeds, by the indication of the clause about which it is predicated, because whenever the phrase "mathal of such-and-such" is used, what is meant is a particular state of it, explained by the discourse; this is from the concision that is obligatory in speech.

So his saying "a'maluhum" (their deeds) is the second subject (mubtada' thani), and "ka-ramadin" (like ashes) is its predicate, and the clause is a predicate of the first subject.

Since "a'maluhum" was made the predicate of "mathal alladhina kafaru," the discourse came to mean that the likeness of the deeds of those who disbelieve is like ashes.

The gathered, numerous deeds were likened to piled-up ashes: when winds strike the ashes, they scatter and disperse in a way that their reassembly is not hoped for. The point of resemblance is the condition resulting from the dissolution of a great quantity after its gathering, and the likened condition is intellectual (ma'qulah).

Page 213
Describing the day as stormy (ʿasif) is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli), meaning its wind is stormy, as one says "a rainy day," meaning its clouds.

Ramad (ashes) is what remains of the burning of firewood and charcoal. ʿAsif has already occurred in His saying ﴿A violent wind came upon them﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surat Yunus.

Among the subtleties of this illustration is that the likeness was chosen to be the condition of gathered ashes, because ashes are the trace of the most excellent deeds of those who disbelieve and the most widespread among them, which is hospitality to guests, until the abundance of ashes became a metaphor in their language for generosity.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read ﴿ashtadat bihi al-riyah﴾ (the winds), and the rest read ﴿ashtadat bihi al-rih﴾ in the singular; both are the same, because the definiteness is generic definiteness (ta'rif al-jins).

The clause ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ is an explanation of the simile clause, meaning: their deeds went to waste, so they have no ability to benefit from any of them.

The clause ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾ is a comprehensive concluding summary of the essence of their state, namely that it is a far-reaching error.

By "al-ba'id" (far-reaching) is meant reaching the utmost limit of what its quiddity attains, that is, far in the distances of error; it is like your saying "the utmost of error" or "the extreme of error." This has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly strayed far astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 116] in Surat al-Nisa'.

[Page 214]

It is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) arising from the statement ﴿So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers"﴾ [Ibrahim: 13]. The destruction of a whole group that is extremely strong and firm is a striking matter, and it raises the question in people's minds:

[Page 215 follows the text below]

How can a group like these be destroyed? The answer is that God, who was able to create the heavens and the earth in their greatness, is able to destroy what is less than them. So the beginning of this resumption is His statement ﴿If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation﴾.

The clause ﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth?﴾ serves as the reason (*ta'lil*) for the resumptive clause. It is placed before it, just as the conclusion is placed before its proof in rhetoric (*khitabah*) and debate (*jidal*).
