Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 21:

﴿And they will come forth before Allah all together. Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed, we were your followers, so can you avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?" They will say: "Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾ [Ibrahim: 19], considering the answer of the condition, which is the taking away. In the speech there is an ellipsis, as the estimated meaning is: "So He took them away, and they came forth before Allah all together," that is, on the Day of Resurrection.

The apparent expectation would have been that he say: "and they will come forth before Allah," but he turned from the present tense to the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, as if it had already occurred, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

Page 216

Al-buruz (coming forth) is going out from a place that conceals, such as a house or a town, and the meaning is: they were gathered from the graves.
And "jamiʿan" (all together) is an emphasis so that it includes all of them, from leaders and masses alike.

In this verse there is a description of the state of the groups on the Day of Resurrection, the disputation of the people of misguidance with their leaders, the disputation of all of them with Satan, and the fact that the believers are occupied away from that by the abode of honour. The purpose of this is to alert people to rectify their condition before it is too late. Thus the intent is warning against what leads to an evil end.

The preposition lam attached to the divine name makes the verb "barazu" (they came forth) transitive to the object it governs. It is said: "baraza li-fulan" when he became manifest to him, that is, presented himself before him, just as it is said: "zahara lahu" (it appeared to him).

Al-du'afaʾ (the weak) are the common people and the followers, and those who were arrogant are the leaders, because they behave arrogantly towards people in general, and arrogance was the emblem of leaders. The sin and ta' (in istakbaru) are for intensification in the sense of pride. Al-tabaʿ (the followers) is a collective noun, the singular being tabiʿ, like khadam and khawal (servants). The fa' (in "fa-hal") is for making the arrogance a consequence of the state of following, since that is a cause requiring intercession for them.

The reason for placing the subject before the predicate in ﴿fa-hal antum mughnūna ʿannā﴾ is that what is asked about is whether those who were arrogant can avail them, not the bare fact of availing them, because they had despaired of it when they saw the signs of the divine wrath upon them and upon their leaders. This is also indicated by the reported words of the arrogant: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently; for us there is no escape﴾, for they knew that they had deceived them in the world. Therefore it is settled that the interrogation is used in the sense of reproach, rebuke and censure, that is: "Display your standing with Allah which you used to claim and with which you deceived us in the world." So placing the subject before the interrogative particle is an indication that it is a non-literal interrogation, and what clarifies this is what occurs in its parallel in Surah Ghafir: ﴿And when they dispute in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed, we were your followers, so can you avail us any portion of the Fire?" Those who were arrogant will say: "Indeed, we are all in it. Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants"﴾ [Ghafir: 47].

The "min" in ﴿min ʿadhab Allah﴾ is substitutive, meaning: availing instead of the punishment of Allah.

Page 217

The "min" in His saying "min shay'" is superfluous, since what follows it falls within the context of interrogation with the particle hal. And "shay'" carries the sense of a verbal noun, whose proper case is the accusative as an absolute object, but it was put in the genitive by the superfluous preposition. The meaning is: "Can you avail us anything?"

The reply of the arrogant is an apology for their deception: they did not intend by it to entangle their followers; how could they, when they had entangled themselves too? That is: "Had we been able to benefit, we would have benefited ourselves." This reply proceeds according to the sense of the reproachful, rebuking interrogation, since they did not answer them by saying "We possess no availing for you," but instead began with an apology for what had come from them towards them in the world, knowing that the weak are aware that they cannot avail them anything against the punishment.

The clause ﴿It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently﴾ is the speech of those who were arrogant. It is a resumptive clause explaining a question from the weak, who seek a ruling from the arrogant on whether to endure or to lament, seeking deliverance from the punishment. So they wished to despair them of that, saying: lamenting profits us nothing, nor does enduring; there is no salvation from the punishment. The pronoun of the speaker "we" includes both the speakers and the respondents, and they gathered themselves together to complete the apology for their deception.

Al-jaza' (lamenting) is grief mixed with agitation. As for al-sabr (endurance), it has already been discussed.

The clause ﴿for us there is no escape﴾ stands in the position of a causal explanation for the meaning of equality, that is: since there is no escape and no salvation, lamenting and enduring are alike.

Al-mahis is a noun of place or verbal noun of the mimi pattern like al-maghib and al-mashib, and it means salvation. It is said: "hasa ʿanhu," meaning he escaped from it. It may also be a noun of place from the same root, meaning: we have no refuge or place in which we might be saved.

[Page 218]

﴿And Satan will say, when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you. I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieve in your having associated me [with Allah] before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment."﴾

The discourse of the weak ones and their leaders, concerning their deception into misguidance, led to the speech of the source of misguidance, who is Satan. This happened either because, after their leaders had excused themselves to them by citing their being deprived of guidance, they knew that the cause of their being led astray was Satan, since negating guidance is equivalent to misguidance. Or because the arrogant ones moved from excusing themselves to the weak ones to blaming Satan, who whispered to them what necessitated their misguidance. All of this happens with a knowledge that arises in their souls like an intuitive awareness. Moreover, His saying ﴿So do not blame me﴾ shows that explicit blame was directed at him. It is also possible that he anticipated it and warded it off before it occurred, and that it is directed at him by way of allusion (ta'rid). So the clause ﴿And Satan will say﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿Then the weak will say﴾ [Ibrahim: 21].

The purpose of describing this situation is to arouse hatred of Satan in the souls of the people of disbelief, so that they may take precaution by repelling his whisperings. This is because this address that Satan directs at them is full of his concealed evil toward them, in what he promised them in the world. Its nature is to provoke their anger at his deception of them and his mockery of them. This produces in them aversion toward him and ill opinion of what they expect him to bring upon them. This is a great principle in admonition and moral training.

The meaning of ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ is: the affair has been completed, that is, by the permission and judgment of Allah. Its completion is its manifestation, which is His command to separate the people of misguidance from the people of guidance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾ [Ya-Sin: 59]. This is done by directing each group to its abode that it deserved by its deeds. Then Satan takes it upon himself to lighten the blame on his own self by associating with himself those whom he misguided, in the responsibility for their misguidance. Allah made him speak this in order to proclaim the truth, and as a testimony against them that they had an acquisition (kasb) in choosing to be impressed by the call to misguidance rather than the call to truth. This is similar to the testimony of their tongues, hands and feet concerning what they used to do, and their saying to them ﴿Allah, who made everything speak, has made us speak﴾ [Fussilat: 21]. It is a manifestation of the reality, a recording against the people of misguidance, and a suppression of their sophistry.

Allah informed people of this out of thoroughness in conveyance, so that people may know comprehensively all that will befall them, and to awaken them so that they may reflect on hidden realities until they become clear and evident. So Satan's saying ﴿So do not blame me; blame yourselves﴾ is a nullification of singling him out for blame, or a refusal to begin directing blame at him, while in fact they are more deserving of blame, or more deserving of having it directed at them first.

As for the effect of Satan's words on the souls of those he addressed, it causes regret in their souls, as an increase in the torment of the self.

The annexation of ﴿promise﴾ to ﴿truth﴾ is an annexation of the qualified noun to its adjective, for the sake of emphasizing the attribute. That is: the true promise that has no breaking of it.

Here ﴿truth﴾ carries the meaning of sincerity and fulfilment of what was promised. Its opposite is breaking (ikhlaf). For this reason he said ﴿and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you﴾, that is, I lied about my promise. The promise of truth includes all that Allah promised them through the Qur'an, upon the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ. The breaking includes all that Satan used to promise them upon the tongues of his allies, and he promises them nothing except delusion.

Al-sultan (authority) is a verbal noun from (tasallata ʿalayhi), meaning he overpowered him and subdued him. That is: I was not compelling you to follow me in what I commanded you.

The exception in ﴿except that I called you﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', i.e., an exception where what follows the particle of exception is not of the same kind as what precedes it). The meaning is: rather, I called you and you responded to me.

From this follows ﴿So do not blame me; blame yourselves﴾. The intended meaning is: blame yourselves, that is, since you accepted my hint and my call. Its explanation was already given at the beginning of the discussion on this verse.

[Page 220]

The two clauses together convey the meaning of restriction (qasr), as if he said: "Do not blame anyone except yourselves." This is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb) with respect to singling him out for blame, whereas what is due to them is that he be associated with them. So the reversal is of their belief that he is singled out, without consideration of partnership. This is one of the rare meanings of relative restriction (qasr idafi), and it is based on considering which of the two sides is more deserving of rejection. That is the side of believing the opposite, to the point that association becomes as if nullified, because the greater share belongs to one of the two partners.

The clause ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾ is an explanation of the clause prohibiting blame, because his being blamed contains an allusion that they were seeking from him a stratagem for their salvation. So he negated that from himself after forbidding them from blaming him.

Al-israakh (helping) means rescue (al-ighatha), derived from al-sarakh (a cry), because the one seeking help cries out at the top of his voice. Hence it is said: asrakhahu, when he answered his cry, just as they said: a'taba-hu, when he accepted his request for pardon. As for the conjunction of ﴿nor can you help me﴾, the intended purpose of it is to emphasize the complete lack of benefit of each of the two for the other.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿bi-musrikhiyya﴾ with a fathah on the yā' and a shaddah. Its original form is bi-musrikhiyi, with two yā's: the first is the yā' of the masculine plural in the genitive case, and the second is the yā' of the first-person speaker. The latter should be sukun, but when the two yā's met, both unvocalized, the avoidance of meeting two unvocalized letters was achieved by a fathah, because the fathah is lighter.

Ḥamzah and Khalaf read ﴿bi-musrikhiyya﴾ with a kasrah on the yā', to avoid meeting two unvocalized letters by a kasrah, because the kasrah is the original means of avoiding such a meeting. Al-Farra' said: moving the yā' with a kasrah is because it is the original means of avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters, except that kasrah on the yā' of the speaker in such a position is rare. He cited in illustration of this avoidance by kasrah the verse of al-Aghlab al-ʿIjli:

He said to her: "Have you [any desire], O Ta-fi?"
She said to him: "You are not one who is pleased."

He meant: "Do you have [any inclination] toward 'O you' (yā hādhihi)?"

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: Quṭrub claimed that it is the dialect of Banu Yarbu'. It is also reported from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' that he permitted the kasrah. All agree that avoidance by fathah in such a position is more well-known than avoidance by kasrah, although avoidance by kasrah is the analogical form [page 221] and the transmission of Ḥamzah's reading has established it. Al-Zajjaj took a harsh stance against it, and al-Zamakhshari followed him. Abu ʿUbayd, al-Akhfash ibn Saʿid and Ibn al-Nahhas preceded them both in this. Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari did not know the attribution of that verse to al-Aghlab al-ʿIjli.

What appears to me is that this reading was recited by Banu Yarbu' of Tamim, and Banu ʿIjl ibn Lujaym of Bakr ibn Wa'il. They read according to their dialect, taking advantage of the concession granted to tribes to recite the Qur'an according to their dialects. This is the concession to which the saying of the Prophet ﷺ alludes: "Indeed, this Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, so recite what is easy of it." This was mentioned in the sixth introduction among the introductions of this exegesis. Then that concession was abrogated by the Prophet's ﷺ recitation in the last years of his blessed life. Nothing has been established that abrogates it in this verse. The matter settled on accepting every reading whose transmission is sound, which agrees with a form in Arabic, and which does not contradict the script of the Imam Mushaf. These conditions are fulfilled in this reading of Ḥamzah, as you have just learned. Its utmost status is that it is treated as what an eloquent Arab speaks according to the dialect of his tribe, such that if it were recited with it in prayer, it would be valid according to Malik and his companions.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I disbelieve in your having associated me [with Allah] before﴾ is a new (istinafi) clause of another disavowal of the consequences of their worshipping him. It is intended to repel an increase of punishment from him by displaying submission to Allah, exalted is He. By his saying (kafartu, "I disbelieved") he meant the intensity of disassociation from their associating him in worship. If by the past tense of (kafartu) he means the past of all times, that is: I was never pleased with your associating me [with Allah], then it is a lie from him, by which he displayed humility. If what he means by the past tense is the establishment of non-approval of their associating him, then it is a regret that serves the function of repentance, at a time when repentance is not accepted. On both interpretations, ﴿before﴾ is connected to ﴿you associated me﴾.

The association that he disbelieved in is their associating him in worship, by their worshipping him alongside Allah. This is because some of the polytheists worship devils and jinn. Those worship the species of Satan directly. Others worship idols, and they worship the devils indirectly, by worshipping his deities.

[Page 222]

The clause ﴿Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment﴾ is part of the speech reported from Satan, and it has the position of a causal explanation for what preceded in his saying ﴿I cannot help you﴾. That is: since no helper can avert punishment from you, it falls upon you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 23:

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be, "Peace."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And they will come forth before Allah, all of them﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. It is a transition to describing the state of the believers on that Day, occasioned by the mention of the state of the polytheists, because the state of the believers on that Day is among the states intended for description, to show the disparity between conditions. Thus the believers on that Day do not enter into the dispute and the contention, out of exalting them above immersing themselves in that turmoil, along with an indication that they are at that time in safety and tranquility.

It is also permissible to make the waw (wa) one of circumstance (li-l-hal), meaning: they came forth, and the weak said, and the arrogant said, and the Satan said, etc., while those who believed and did righteous deeds had already been admitted into gardens. In that case it is an indication that they attained the abode of honour at the very first moment.

His saying "by the permission of their Lord" (bi-idhni rabbihim) is an indication of care and concern; it is thus more specific than the general matter of the decree (al-qada' al-ʿamm).

His saying ﴿their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾ has had its parallel mentioned earlier, at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 24–26:

Page 223
﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents an example: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly established and whose branches reach into the sky, giving its fruit at all times by the permission of its Lord. And Allah presents examples for the people that they may be reminded.﴾ ﴿And the example of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾

This is a fresh beginning (istiʼnaf ibtidaʼi), required by the connection with what was related about the conditions of the people of misguidance and the conditions of the people of guidance, beginning from His saying, ﴿And they will come forth before Allah all together﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], up to His saying, ﴿Their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾ [Ibrahim: 23]. Allah thus presents an example for the word of faith and the word of polytheism. His saying, ﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents an example﴾, is an alerting of the mind, so that it may anticipate what comes after this statement. This is like the speech, "Do you not know?" This example had not been presented before the revelation of the verse; rather, the verse itself brought it. The statement is therefore an incitement to learn this example. The formulation of this incitement in the past tense, indicated by the particle (lam), which negates the verb in the past, and by the verb (ḍaraba) in the past form, is intended to increase the incitement to know this example and what it represents.

The interrogation in "Have you not considered" is either reproachful (inkari), addressing the listener as if he did not know, so that his lack of knowledge is rebuked; or it is used to express astonishment at the lack of knowledge of this matter, although the motives for knowing it are abundant; or it is for affirmation (taqrir), and examples of this in affirmation are many. It is a metonymy for urging knowledge of this matter.

The address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The seeing is cognitive (ʻilmiyya), its verb suspended from operating on what follows it by the interrogative (kayfa). The choice of (kayfa) here indicates that the manner of presenting this example is marvelous in its eloquence and its applicability.

The example appeared in His saying, ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Presenting an example (darb al-mathal): the composition of its structure that indicates the likening of a condition. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿that Allah is not ashamed to present an example, whatever it may be﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Page 224
The attribution of (ḍaraba) to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because Allah revealed it to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

Since the example is a meaning comprising several things, it was sufficient to leave the verb (ḍaraba) attached to it in a general manner, which is explained by His saying, ﴿a good word, like a tree﴾ and so on to the end. Thus "kalimatan" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "mathalan": a detailed substitute for a general term. The example is connected to it, because of what the genitive construction in its counterpart in His saying, ﴿and the example of an evil word﴾, implies.

It has been said that the good word is the word of Islam, which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; and the evil word is the word of polytheism.

"Good" (ṭayyiba) means beneficial. The word "good" was used metaphorically for benefit because of its pleasing effect on souls, like the effect of pleasant fragrances. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿and they sailed with them with a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surat Yunus.

The branch (farʻ) is what extends from a thing and rises, derived from iftirāʻ, which is elevation. The branch of a tree is its bough, and the root of a tree is its base.

"Sky" (samāʼ) is used for height, and this adds to the tree's radiance and beauty of appearance.

"Ukl" with a dammah on the hamzah is that which is eaten, and its attribution to the pronoun of the tree is in the sense of (lām, belonging). It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿and We favor some of them over others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4] in Surat al-Ra'd.

Thus the thing likened is the condition resulting from radiance in sensation and joy in the soul, and the increase of the roots of benefit through the acquisition of successive benefits in the manner of a firmly established root, and beauty of appearance, and the growth of branches, and abundance of fruit, and the pleasure of eating it. Each part of one of the two conditions corresponds to the other part of the second condition; and this is the most complete state of an illustration, that it be capable of combining the likeness and dividing it.

The same applies to the depiction of the condition of the evil word by the evil tree, in the opposite manner, with all the qualities mentioned earlier: disturbance of belief, constriction of the chest, turbidity of thought, and successive harm. The illustration has been abbreviated here, by suffice with the opposite, so all the benefits of the good word are negated from it.

Page 225

What is meant by it is the statements of the Qur'an, since its meanings are true and its proof is clear. Thus the definite article in al-qawl is for comprehensiveness of all firm statements, and the bāʾ in "bi-l-qawl" is causal (lil-sababiyyah).

The meaning of Allah firming up those who believe by it is that Allah facilitates for them the understanding of the divine statements in their proper manner and the perception of their proofs, until their hearts are at rest with them, no doubt having crept into them, and they become firm in their faith, not shaken by it, not wavering.

This takes place through many manifestations in which their firmness in the truth appears, in speech and in conduct, and in which the trial of non-believers appears in all circumstances.

The interpretation of this is by its contrast with His words ﴿and Allah causes the wrongdoers to go astray﴾, i.e., the polytheists, meaning that He places them in bewilderment and blindness in this world and in the Hereafter. Ḍalāl (going astray) is confusion and disorder, and it is therefore the effect appropriate to its cause, namely the word that has been uprooted from above the earth, as the contrast indicates.

Al-ẓālimūn (the wrongdoers): the polytheists. Allah the Exalted says ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 28–29:

﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude and caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin?﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the place of settlement.﴾

After the parable of the two religions, the description of their effects on their adherents follows. The mention of the polytheists' condition came first, because it is more striking, its lesson is more important, and caution is given precedence over adorning oneself with its opposite. Then the condition of the believers is mentioned, with His words ﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], etc.

The interrogative is used here to create eagerness to see this matter.

The "seeing" (ru'yah) here is visual (basariyyah), and its object is something that can be seen. The fact that its verb is followed by (ila) also favors this, as in His words ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

The addressee has been placed in the position of one who has not seen, while the address is to one who is capable of contemplating the condition of these people who exchanged the favor of Allah, given the clarity of their condition.

Kufr (disbelief) here means ingratitude for the blessing, which is the opposite of gratitude (shukr), and associating partners with Allah is among the ingratitude for His blessing.

In His words ﴿exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude﴾ there is an elegant ellipsis (ihtibak), and the sense of the sentence is: they exchanged the favor of Allah and its thanks for disbelief in it and a punishment from Him, as indicated by His words ﴿and caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin﴾, etc.

The word "exchange" (tabdil) is used metaphorically for placing a thing in the position that another thing deserves, because it resembles the exchange of one essence for another essence. Those who made this exchange are a well-known group, as indicated by the context of His words ﴿Have you not seen those who﴾. They are those who received the wicked word from Satan, that is, the word of polytheism, and they are those among the polytheists of Makkah who were arrogant, who obstinately opposed the call of Islam, denied the Prophet ﷺ, drove out whomever they could, and were the cause of their people's settling in the abode of ruin. Therefore the attribution of the verb "caused to settle" to them is in the manner of metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (al-majaz al-'aqli).

The favor of Allah that they exchanged is the favor that He settled them in His sanctuary, granted them security in their travelling and their residence, made the hearts of people yearn toward them, and protected them from what befell others of wars, raids and aggression. Yet they disbelieved in the One who bestowed these blessings and worshipped stones. Then Allah bestowed His favor upon them by sending among them the best of His prophets ﷺ and guiding them to the truth, and preparing for them the means of leadership and salvation in this world and the Hereafter. But they exchanged the thanks for that with disbelief in it. Thus the greatest favor of Allah is the message of Muhammad ﷺ, and the call of Ibrahim and his progeny, peace be upon them.

"Their people" (qawmuhum) are those who followed them in persisting in disbelief until they died as disbelievers, so they are most deserving of being attributed to them.

Al-bawar is ruin and loss, and its "abode" (dar) is the place in which it occurred.

To "cause to settle" (ihlal) in it means to cause to descend into it. The intended meaning of ihlal is causation of it: that is, they were the cause of their people's settling in the abode of ruin, which is Hell in the Hereafter, and the places of killing and disgrace in this world such as the site of Badr. Thus "the abode of ruin" may be Hell, and this is how 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas and many scholars explained it. It may also be the land of Badr, which is a report from 'Ali and from Ibn 'Abbas.

The use of the past tense in "caused to settle" is for the sake of affirming certainty, because the time of the settling is later, since the surah is Makki.

By "those who exchanged the favor of Allah" and "caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin" is meant the chiefs of the polytheists of Quraysh. So, according to the interpretation of "the abode of ruin" as the abode of ruin in the Hereafter, His words "Hell" are a substitute (badal) for "the abode of ruin," and the clause "which they will burn in" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "Hell." Thus "the abode of ruin" is restricted to its greatest instance, which is the Fire, and this is taken as mentioning some instances for their importance.

According to the interpretation of "the abode of ruin" as the land of Badr, His words "Hell, which they will burn in" form a new independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the accusative of "Hell" is as an object of a verb omitted, indicated by the verb "they will burn in," by way of the construction of preoccupation (ishtighal).

As for what is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, that those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude are the two wicked families of Quraysh: the Banu Umayyah and the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Makhzum. He said: "As for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time; and as for the Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficient against them on the day of Badr." I do not think this is anything but the fabrication of some hostile people opposed to the Banu Umayyah. In narrations from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, it is reported that he said: "They are the disbelievers of Quraysh." Neither 'Umar nor 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, meant those of the Banu Umayyah who embraced Islam, for no Muslim would say that. So beware of erroneous understandings. Likewise is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas:

that they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those of the Arabs who followed him, who became Christians in the time of 'Umar and settled in the lands of the Romans. If this is authentically reported from him, then his statement is in the sense of analogy and illustration; otherwise, how could they be the intended meaning of the verse? This only occurred in the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

The clause "and wretched is the place of settlement" is conjoined to the clause "which they will burn in," or is a circumstantial clause from "Hell," and the implied sense is: "and wretched is the place of settlement it is."

Thus "the abode of ruin" may be Hell, and this is how 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas and many scholars explained it. It may also be the land of Badr, which is a report from 'Ali and from Ibn 'Abbas.

The use of the past tense in "caused to settle" is for the sake of affirming certainty, because the time of the settling is later, since the surah is Makki.

By "those who exchanged the favor of Allah" and "caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin" is meant the chiefs of the polytheists of Quraysh. So, according to the interpretation of "the abode of ruin" as the abode of ruin in the Hereafter, His words "Hell" are a substitute (badal) for "the abode of ruin," and the clause "which they will burn in" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "Hell." Thus "the abode of ruin" is restricted to its greatest instance, which is the Fire, and this is taken as mentioning some instances for their importance.

According to the interpretation of "the abode of ruin" as the land of Badr, His words "Hell, which they will burn in" form a new independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the accusative of "Hell" is as an object of a verb omitted, indicated by the verb "they will burn in," by way of the construction of preoccupation (ishtighal).

As for what is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, that those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude are the two wicked families of Quraysh: the Banu Umayyah and the Banu al-Mughirah ibn Makhzum. He said: "As for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time; and as for the Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficient against them on the day of Badr." I do not think this is anything but the fabrication of some hostile people opposed to the Banu Umayyah. In narrations from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, it is reported that he said: "They are the disbelievers of Quraysh." Neither 'Umar nor 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, meant those of the Banu Umayyah who embraced Islam, for no Muslim would say that. So beware of erroneous understandings. Likewise is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas:

that they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those of the Arabs who followed him, who became Christians in the time of 'Umar and settled in the lands of the Romans. If this is authentically reported from him, then his statement is in the sense of analogy and illustration; otherwise, how could they be the intended meaning of the verse? This only occurred in the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

The clause "and wretched is the place of settlement" is conjoined to the clause "which they will burn in," or is a circumstantial clause from "Hell," and the implied sense is: "and wretched is the place of settlement it is."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 30:**

﴿And they set up rivals to God in order to lead others astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with *baddalū* and *aḥallū* (in the preceding verse), so the pronoun refers to *alladhīna* ("those who"), namely the leaders of polytheism. The act of *jaʿl* ("setting up") is true of inventing this practice, as ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy of Khuzaʿa did, and it is also true of establishing it, spreading it, and arguing for it, such as the people of Mecca placing the idols in the Kaaba and putting Hubal on its roof.

*Al-andād* is the plural of *nidd* (with a kasra on the nūn), meaning one who is equal in glory and eminence. It was discussed earlier, at God's words ﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾ [al-Baqara 2:22], in surah al-Baqara.

The majority of readers recite *li-yuḍillū* (لِيُضِلُّوا) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, from *aḍalla* ("to cause someone else to go astray"), meaning making him astray. Here leading astray is given as the cause of their setting up rivals to God, even though they did not intend to mislead people. Rather, they intended aims that are equivalent to misleading, since these aims caused people to fall into error. So the outcome of misleading is expressed through misleading itself, because it leads to it even if they did not intend it. It is as if it were said: "in order to go astray from His way," as a condemnation of them through the extreme nature of their action. They did not lead others astray without themselves having gone astray. Thus it is understood that they went astray and led others astray, and this is a form of concision (*ījāz*).

Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Ruways from Yaʿqūb recite *li-yaḍillū* (لِيَضِلُّوا) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, meaning: "so that their going astray may continue." When they set up the rivals, their going astray was already present at the time of the action. The meaning of the causal *lām* (*lām al-taʿlīl*, the "lām of purpose") is that the verb is in the future, because it is in the sense of (*an*) in the verbal-noun construction (*al-maṣdariyya*) after the *lām* of purpose. It is known that they led people astray from His words *and made their people abide in the house of ruin*.

"The way of God" (*sabīl Allāh*) is every action that proceeds in accordance with what pleases God. The action is likened to a road that leads to the destination. This has been discussed more than once before.

The clause ﴿Say: "Enjoy yourselves"﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanation (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a new sentence that answers an implied question). The addressee of ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged﴾ [Ibrāhīm 14:28], when he learns these conditions, asks about the recompense appropriate to their crime, and how God left them to revel in blessings. So it is answered that they will go to the Fire, that is, they will die and then go to the punishment.

He was commanded to convey this to them, because they used to boast that they were in luxury and dominance. This is like His words: ﴿Do not let the movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you. It is a small enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ in surah Āl ʿImrān [3:196–197].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 31:

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾

This is a resumed statement (isti'naf) arising from the mention of the state of the group upon whom the evil word was made binding, by mentioning the state of its counterpart, namely the group upon whom the good word was made binding. When the discourse began with the first group, for the purpose of admonition and disassociation, it was followed by the second group in the manner of an interjection (i'tiraድ) between the aims of the speech, as will come in the verse following it.

A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Isra': "And they said, 'When we are bones and crumbled remains, will we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?' Say, 'Be stones or iron,'" until He said: ﴿And say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra': 53].

When they were adorned with perfection, the address concerning them was phrased with the designation of being described as believers, and with the form of command regarding what they were already engaged in, namely prayer and spending, for the purpose of persistence in that. Thus the placing of this verse after the one before it has a suitable connection, owing to the contrast between the two states.

Since the believers already establish prayer and already spend, it is determined that the intended meaning is seeking an increase in that. For this reason the present tense was chosen together with an implied imperative lam (lam al-amr), rather than the imperative verb form, because the present tense indicates renewal; with the lam of command it corresponds to the state of one who is clothed in the act that he is commanded to perform. This differs from the form (if'al), whose origin is a request for bringing about the act commanded from one who is not yet engaged in it. Thus the original of yuqimu al-salat is li-yuqimu, and the lam of command was deleted for lightness.

This is the subtle point of the occurrence of such a construction in the places where it occurs, as in this verse and in His saying "And say to My servants that they should say that which is best" in Surat al-Isra'; that is, "Say to them: let them establish, and let them say," and so it is reported in meaning.

In my view, among this category is His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Hijr: "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; but they will come to know" [al-Hijr: 3], that is, leave them so that they may eat and enjoy themselves and hope may distract them. It is then used in the sense of respite and threat. For this reason we are certain that these verbs are governed by an implied lam of command. This is the view of al-Kisa'i when a jussive verb follows the lam of command that is deleted after the verb "say" (qul) has preceded it, as in Mughni al-Labib; and Ibn Malik agreed with him in his commentary on al-Kafiyah. Some have said: the jussive of the present verb in response to the imperative "say" is due to an implied verb, the thing said, indicated by what follows it, and the estimate is: "Say to My servants: establish, and they will establish; and spend, and they will spend." Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Malik said that this applies specifically to what occurs after an imperative of speech, as in this verse; and they overlooked examples like the verse "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves" and ﴿and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26] of what We have provided them, as a reminder of the blessing, as an exhortation to spending, so that it may be thanks for the blessing.

"Secretly and publicly" are two circumstantial accusatives (hal) from the pronoun in yunfiqu, and both are verbal nouns (masdar). This was already discussed at His saying "secretly and publicly" in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended purpose is to generalise the conditions in seeking spending, lest they think that public declaration leads to ostentation, as was the state in the Jahiliyyah, or that spending in secret leads to concealing the bounty of God by the rich, and so leads to ingratitude for the blessing. Perhaps a person chooses one of the two states and so leaves off spending in the other state, and much benefit and great reward are lost. So God made clear to people that spending is righteousness which is not spoiled by the circumstances surrounding it, and that actions are by intentions. Something of this has already been mentioned at His saying: "Those who criticise those among the believers who give voluntarily in charity and those who find nothing but their own effort," the verse.

It has been said that what is meant by "secret" is voluntary spending, and by "public" is obligatory spending.

The placing of "secret" before "public" is an indication that it is the better of the two states, because it is further from the thoughts of ostentation; and because in it there is preservation of some of the modesty of the one who receives the charity.

His saying ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade﴾ and what follows is connected to the verb ﴿establish the prayer and spend﴾, that is: that they should do those two matters before the arrival of the Day on which exchanges and spending are impossible. This is a metonymy for the great benefits of establishing prayer and spending before the Day of Recompense, when they will wish that they had increased in those two, because of what would gladden them of their reward; yet they will find no way to seek increase from them, since on that Day there is no trade by which reward is bought, and no friendship, whose nature is to supply and aid with reward. Thus "trade" means exchange, and "friendship" is a metonymy for voluntary giving.

His saying, Exalted is He, parallel to this: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided you before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, no friendship, and no intercession﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254], in Surat al-Baqarah.

By this it becomes clear that what is meant by "friendship" here is its effects, by the context; and the intended meaning is not the negation of friendship (khullah), that is companionship and affection, because affection is established among the pious. He, Exalted is He, said:

﴿Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. And the negation of trade and friendship, which are the means of bounty and support, suffices for the negation of seeking increase.

The introduction of the particle of genitive (harf al-jarr) upon a noun of time, namely "before" (qabl), is to emphasise priority, so that the sense of hastening is understood.

The majority read "la bay'un" with nominative (raf'), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the fathah construction; these are two readings in the negation of an indefinite noun by the particle "la".

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), serving as an argument for what the phrase ﴿And they set up rivals to God﴾ [Ibrahim: 30] implies. It is separated from what it argues for by the phrase ﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish the prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], and within the argument is embedded an enumeration of blessings that deserve gratitude, so that the state of those who disbelieved in them becomes evident, and by contrast the state of those who gave thanks for them, and so that the thankful may increase in gratitude. The primary aim is therefore to argue against the people of ignorance (jahiliyya), as is shown by what follows it in the words ﴿And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. In this verse, then, are mentioned general, visible, tangible blessings that cannot be denied, but their purpose is to remind that the one who bestows them and brings them into being is God, exalted is He.

[Page 235 continues]

The discourse opens with the name of the Creator, because specifying Him is the most important aim, and it is predicated with a relative clause (al-mawsul), because the relative clause is known to be attributed to Him and established for Him, since the polytheists do not dispute that God is the one who creates, nor do they claim that the idols create anything, as He said: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God﴾ [Luqman: 25]. Thus the creation of the heavens and the earth is a proof of the divinity of their Creator and a preparation for the blessings deposited in them. The sending down of water from the sky to the earth, the bringing forth of fruits from the earth, the seas and rivers from the earth, the sun and moon from the sky, and night and day from the sky and from the earth, and the explanation of these blessings has already passed in earlier verses.

Provision (rizq) is sustenance (qut). Subjugation (taskhir) in its literal sense is making something submissive and compliant; it is a metaphor for making a thing that is not rational amenable to the disposal of another. It has already been discussed at His words ﴿And the sun, the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in Surat al-A'raf. His words ﴿so that it may run in the sea﴾ state the reason for the subjugation of its making.

The meaning of the subjugation of the ship is that its very nature is subjugated, through inspiring humans to build it and shape it in a manner that runs upon the sea without any hindrance.

His words "by His command" (bi-amrihi) are connected to "runs" (tajri).

Here "command" (amr) means permission, that is, the facilitation of its running on the sea, through restraining storms from it and assisting it with the gentle wind. This is like His words ﴿Do you not see that God has subjected to you what is in the earth, and the ship that runs on the sea by His command?﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. He expressed this command as a blessing in His words ﴿Do you not see that the ship runs on the sea by the blessing of God?﴾ [Luqman: 31], and the verse ﴿And among His signs are the ships on the sea like mountains; if He wills, He stills the winds, and they remain motionless upon its surface﴾ [al-Shura: 32] has explained it.

The subjugation of the rivers is their creation in such a manner that the water moves from place to place and settles in some low-lying areas, so that whoever passes by it drinks from it, and [people] settle on its banks where its waters remain.

[Page 236]

Some of them He created with a permanent course, such as the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Nile, for drinking and for the passage of ships upon them.

The subjugation of the sun and moon is their creation in conditions suited to humanity's benefit from their light and to regulating their times by their movement.

The meaning of "constantly" (da'ibayn) is that they continue in states that do not change, for if they varied, humans would not be able to regulate them, and they would fall into bewilderment and doubt.

Fulk (ships) is a collective noun whose form is the same as its singular, and it has already been discussed at His words ﴿and the ships that run on the sea with what benefits people﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara.

The meaning of ﴿And He gave you of everything you asked Him for﴾ is that He gave you a portion of all your desired things that lie outside your own acquisition, such that your part is to ask God for them. This includes the breeding of livestock, the bringing forth of fruits and grains, and the warding off of afflictions from all of these, such as warding off diseases from livestock and calamities from fruits and grains.

Thus the clause ﴿And He gave you of everything you asked Him for﴾ is a generalization after a specification, and so it stands in the position of a concluding clause (tadhyil) for what precedes it, for wisdoms that God knows and that they do not know: ﴿If God were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely act arrogantly on the earth; but He sends down in measure what He wills; indeed He is All-Aware, All-Seeing of His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 27]. Also, bestowal and grace are in proportion to giving, not in proportion to deprivation. With this, the explanation of the verse becomes clear.

The clause ﴿And if you count God's blessing, you cannot number it﴾ is an emphasis of the concluding clause and an increase in generality, serving as a warning that much of what God has given them is known, while much of it they do not comprehend or do not remember when they intend to enumerate the blessings.

So the meaning of "if you count" (in ta'uddu) is: if you attempt to count and begin to do so. This includes blessings to which people are accustomed and which they forget are blessings, such as the blessing of the self, the blessing of the senses, the blessing of digesting food and drink, the blessing of blood circulation, and the blessing of health. Here al-Fakhr has an excellent discussion, so consult it.

[Page 237]

Ihsa' (numbering) is the determination of a count. It is derived from hasa, which is a noun for number, and it is transferred from hasa (pebbles), which are small stones, because they used to count large numbers with pebbles to avoid error.

The clause ﴿Indeed, man is surely unjust and ungrateful﴾ is an emphasis of the meaning of the rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) used to establish the transformation of blessing into disbelief. For this reason it is separated from it (fusilat 'anha).

By "man" (al-insan) is meant a category of humankind, namely those characterized by the content of this emphasized clause and its emphasis. Thus "man" here is the polytheist, like the one in His words ﴿And man says: When I am dead, shall I really be brought forth alive?﴾ [Maryam: 66]. This usage is frequent in the Qur'an.

The two intensive forms in ﴿zalum (unjust) and kaffar (ungrateful)﴾ are required by the abundance of blessings implied by His words ﴿If you count God's blessing, you cannot number it﴾, for in proportion to the abundance of blessings, the disbelief of the disbelievers in them increases, since they turned away from worshipping the Benefactor and worshipped what gives them no benefit at all. As for the believers, they do not deny God's blessings nor worship anyone other than Him.

The subjugation of the rivers is their creation in such a manner that the water moves from place to place and settles in some low-lying areas, so that whoever passes by it drinks from it, and [people] settle on its banks where its waters remain.

[Page 236]

Some of them He created with a permanent course, such as the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Nile, for drinking and for the passage of ships upon them.

The subjugation of the sun and moon is their creation in conditions suited to humanity's benefit from their light and to regulating their times by their movement.

The meaning of "constantly" (da'ibayn) is that they continue in states that do not change, for if they varied, humans would not be able to regulate them, and they would fall into bewilderment and doubt.

Fulk (ships) is a collective noun whose form is the same as its singular, and it has already been discussed at His words ﴿and the ships that run on the sea with what benefits people﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara.

The meaning of ﴿And He gave you of everything you asked Him for﴾ is that He gave you a portion of all your desired things that lie outside your own acquisition, such that your part is to ask God for them. This includes the breeding of livestock, the bringing forth of fruits and grains, and the warding off of afflictions from all of these, such as warding off diseases from livestock and calamities from fruits and grains.

Thus the clause ﴿And He gave you of everything you asked Him for﴾ is a generalization after a specification, and so it stands in the position of a concluding clause (tadhyil) for what precedes it, for wisdoms that God knows and that they do not know: ﴿If God were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely act arrogantly on the earth; but He sends down in measure what He wills; indeed He is All-Aware, All-Seeing of His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 27]. Also, bestowal and grace are in proportion to giving, not in proportion to deprivation. With this, the explanation of the verse becomes clear.

The clause ﴿And if you count God's blessing, you cannot number it﴾ is an emphasis of the concluding clause and an increase in generality, serving as a warning that much of what God has given them is known, while much of it they do not comprehend or do not remember when they intend to enumerate the blessings.

So the meaning of "if you count" (in ta'uddu) is: if you attempt to count and begin to do so. This includes blessings to which people are accustomed and which they forget are blessings, such as the blessing of the self, the blessing of the senses, the blessing of digesting food and drink, the blessing of blood circulation, and the blessing of health. Here al-Fakhr has an excellent discussion, so consult it.

[Page 237]

Ihsa' (numbering) is the determination of a count. It is derived from hasa, which is a noun for number, and it is transferred from hasa (pebbles), which are small stones, because they used to count large numbers with pebbles to avoid error.

The clause ﴿Indeed, man is surely unjust and ungrateful﴾ is an emphasis of the meaning of the rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) used to establish the transformation of blessing into disbelief. For this reason it is separated from it (fusilat 'anha).

By "man" (al-insan) is meant a category of humankind, namely those characterized by the content of this emphasized clause and its emphasis. Thus "man" here is the polytheist, like the one in His words ﴿And man says: When I am dead, shall I really be brought forth alive?﴾ [Maryam: 66]. This usage is frequent in the Qur'an.

The two intensive forms in ﴿zalum (unjust) and kaffar (ungrateful)﴾ are required by the abundance of blessings implied by His words ﴿If you count God's blessing, you cannot number it﴾, for in proportion to the abundance of blessings, the disbelief of the disbelievers in them increases, since they turned away from worshipping the Benefactor and worshipped what gives them no benefit at all. As for the believers, they do not deny God's blessings nor worship anyone other than Him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 14, verses 35–36:**

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols."﴾ ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

This is a conjunction with the phrase ﴿Have you not considered those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ [Ibrahim: 28]. Just as they exchanged Allah's favour for ingratitude, they neglected to give thanks for the blessings Allah had settled them in, through the answering of the supplication of their forefather Abraham (peace be upon him). They also exchanged the guidance of their righteous predecessor for the example of their ancestors who were in error, and they exchanged his supplication for their good with ingratitude toward the flow of those blessings.

Page 238

It is also permissible for it to be conjoined with the phrase ﴿Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 32], in that the discourse moved from mention of the general blessings for mankind, under whose favour the people of Mecca fall by virtue of generality, to mention of the blessings which Allah specifically bestowed upon the people of Mecca. It also shifted the style of expressing gratitude for them to the style of relating the words of Abraham, in order to incorporate the honouring of Abraham (peace be upon him) and an allusion to his descendants among the polytheists.

(﴿وإذ﴾) is a noun of past time in the accusative, functioning as the object of a verb that is omitted, as is common in such constructions. Its estimated form is: "Remember when Abraham said," as an added emphasis on the wonder at the state of the polytheists mentioned in His words ﴿Have you not considered those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ [Ibrahim: 28]. Thus the lesson drawn from both situations is the same.

And (﴿رب﴾) is a vocative whose particle of address has been omitted. Its original form is "rabbi" (my Lord), and the ya' of the first person was dropped for lightness, which is common in a vocative attached to the ya' of the speaker.

And (al-balad) means a specific place on the earth, and it is also applied to a town. The definiteness in (al-balad) is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), because it is a known thing by presence. And (al-balad) is an apposition to the demonstrative.

The narration of his supplication without specifying the city is a vagueness that is followed by clarification in His words ﴿by Your Sacred House﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. Or it is a reference to what is known among the Arabs, that it is Mecca. The exegesis of its parallel has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah. The definiteness here is definiteness of reference, whereas the indefiniteness in the verse of al-Baqarah is indefiniteness of kind (tankir al-nau'iyya). So here he supplicated for the city that it be secure, while in the verse of Surah al-Baqarah he supplicated for a referred-to place that Allah make it of the kind of secure cities. Hence the outcome of the two meanings is one.

And (﴿واجنبني﴾) is an imperative from the bare triliteral form. It is said: "jannabahu al-shay'," when one makes it a side away from himself, meaning he distanced it from him. This is the dialect of the people of Najd, while the people of the Hijaz say "jannabahu" with doubling or "ajnabahu" with a hamza. The Qur'an here came in the dialect of the people of Najd because it is lighter.

By "his sons" he meant his direct offspring, who at that time were Isma'il and Ishaq. This is the use of the plural for the dual. Or he meant all of his progeny, generalising in goodness, and so he was answered in part.

Page 239

And (al-asnam) is the plural of (sanam), which is a statue, or a stone, or a structure taken as an object of worship and called a god. Abraham (peace be upon him) meant the likes of Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr, the idols of the people of Noah, and the likes of the idols which the people of Abraham worshipped.

The repetition of the vocative in His words ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray﴾ serves to express grief over that.

The clause ﴿they have led many of the people astray﴾ is a justification for his supplication to keep him away from worshipping them, that they are an error which has circulated among many people. Hence it is right for the believer who is careful about his faith to fear that their trial may sweep him away. Thus the opening of the clause with the particle of emphasis serves the sense of causation that the particle (inna) conveys in this context.

That is because Abraham (peace be upon him) left his land of Ur of the Chaldeans in denunciation of the worshippers of idols, and he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], and he said to his people: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Maryam: 48]. When he passed by Egypt, he found them worshipping idols. Then he entered Palestine and found them worshippers of idols. Then he came to the valley ('Araba) of Tihama and settled his wife there. He found it empty, and around it were the people of Jurhum, a folk upon natural disposition and simplicity. So he settled Hajar and his son Isma'il there. Then he established there the landmark of monotheism, which is the House of Allah, the Ka'ba, which he built with his son Isma'il, and he intended it to be a refuge for monotheism. His son remained there so that he would be a caller to monotheism. Therefore he inevitably asked that this be a secure city, so that its inhabitants would be safe, and so that whoever came to them might be taught the foundations of monotheism.

Upon this he based His words ﴿whoever follows me is of me﴾, meaning: whoever among the people follows me and avoids worshipping idols, he is of me. Thus his father and his people are included in this, and his offspring are included too, because the conditional form is suitable for both past and future.

And the (﴿من﴾) in His words ﴿of me﴾ is (min al-ittisaliyya, of connection), and its original sense is figurative partitive, meaning: he is connected to me with the connection of a part to its whole.

Page 240

And His words ﴿and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ express courtesy in the station of supplication and a benefit to the disobedient among the people to the extent he is able. The meaning is: "As for whoever disobeys me, I entrust his affair to Your mercy and forgiveness." The intent is not a supplication for forgiveness for the one who disobeys. This is from the predominance of forbearance over Abraham (peace be upon him), and from fear of the uprooting of the disobedient among his descendants. For this reason Allah gave them enjoyment for a little while in the life of this world, as His exalted words indicate: ﴿He said: "As for whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], and His words ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me, for indeed He will guide me." And He made it a word remaining among his descendants that they might return﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 26–28], and ﴿Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 29]. The bringing of this supplication here is an allusion to the polytheists among the Arabs, that they did not show dutiful kindness to their father Abraham (peace be upon him).

Since His words ﴿indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ are an entrusting of the matter, it contains no indication that Allah forgives the one who associates partners with Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 37:

﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾

The clause ﴿Indeed I have settled some of my offspring﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʼnafah) introducing another supplication. It is opened with the vocative (al-nida') to increase the humble entreaty (al-tadarru'). The fact that the vocative here repeats an earlier vocative constitutes a kind of linking between sentences opened with the vocative, namely linking like with like (rabt al-mithl bi-mithlih).

The word "Lord" (al-Rabb) is here attached to a plural pronoun, unlike its earlier occurrences, because the supplication with which it opens contains a share (hazz) for the one making the supplication and for his children. It is likely that Isma'il, peace be upon him, was present with him at the time of the supplication, as indicated by another verse: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il, [saying], "Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], up to His saying ﴿and make us Muslims [submitting] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. This is part of the meaning of the gratitude sought here.

The "min" (from) in His saying "min dhurriyyati" (from my offspring) is in the sense of "some of," meaning Isma'il, peace be upon him, who is part of his offspring. This supplication was therefore uttered by Abraham, peace be upon him, after a period from the building of the Ka'bah and the settling of Makkah, as indicated by his saying in this supplication: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Isḥaq﴾ [Ibrahim: 39], where he mentioned Isḥaq, peace be upon him.

The "wadi" is the land between mountains, and it is the valley of Makkah. ﴿Uncultivated﴾ (ghayr dhi zar') is a descriptive qualifier, meaning a valley not suitable for plant growth, because it is rock. The word "dhu" (possessor of) indicates the owner of what it is attached to and his being endowed with it: when one says "dhu mal" (possessor of wealth), the wealth is firmly his. When the opposite is intended, one says "ghayr dhi" followed by the thing, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness﴾ [al-Zumar: 28], meaning that no crookedness affects it. For this usage, he did not say "a valley that is not cultivated" or "with no crops in it."

﴿Near Your Sacred House﴾ ('inda baytika) is a second descriptive qualifier of "wadi," or a circumstantial clause (hal).

The "muharram" (sacred) means that which is protected from the hands reaching it with anything that would corrupt it or harm its people, by what God has placed in the souls of nations of reverence and veneration, and by what they witnessed of the destruction of those who intended to violate it wrongfully with irreligion. The people of the Elephant are not far from them in this.

"Li-yuqimu" (that they may establish) is linked to "asknt" (I have settled): that is, the reason for settling them in that valley near that House is that no preoccupation should distract them from establishing prayer in that House, so that the House remains inhabited forever.

Placing the vocative in the middle serves to give importance to the introduction of the supplication and is an increase in humble entreaty. By this it becomes fitting that he branches the supplication for them upon it, by asking that He make hearts among the people incline toward them, because the aspiration of the righteous is for the establishment of the religion.

"Al-af'idah" (hearts) is the plural of "fu'ad," which is the heart; the intended meaning here is the self and the intellect.

The intended meaning is: "make people who will incline toward them." The word "hearts" is inserted to indicate that the people's coming to them is with longing and love, to the extent that it is as if the one hastening is the heart and not the body.

Since he mentioned "hearts" for this subtle point, it is good for its clarification to state that they are "from the people." So "min" (from) is explanatory (bayaniyyah), not partitive (tab'idiyyah), since there is no benefit in the latter. The meaning: "make people who intend them with the core of their hearts."

"Tahwi" is the present form of "hawa," with an open waw, meaning to fall; here it is used figuratively for hastening in walking, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Like a boulder of rock that the torrent has cast down from a height.*

For this reason it takes the preposition "li-" rather than "ila."

The hastening is used as a metaphor (kinayah) for love and longing to visit them. The purpose of this supplication is to make their place pleasant through the frequent visits of visitors and the fulfilment of their needs by them. The indefinite is absolute and is understood according to what is customary in the prosperity of cities and markets with those who come; therefore he did not restrict it in the supplication with anything indicating abundance, being content with what is well known.

With the people's love for them, love for the land also arises, and repeated visits to it. This is a cause for their finding comfort in it and their desire to establish its rites, so it ultimately leads to calling to the religion.

The hope of their gratitude is included in the supplication, because it is appended as a completion of it, as an approach to being answered, and as an increase in the supplication for them that they may be among the grateful. The intended purpose is the abundance of the means of devoting oneself to worship and the absence of what would come between them and it, such as the trial of toil for earning a livelihood.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 38:

﴿Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal and what we declare. Nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven.﴾

He came with this address to Allah encompassing what was in his heart, and as a concluding summary (fadhlakah) of the preceding sentences, which included mention of the misguidance of many people and mention of those who followed his call and those who disobeyed him. It was also mentioned that he intended, by settling his offspring in Makkah, the hope that they would be guardians of the House of Allah, that they would establish the prayer, and that they would be thankful for the blessings bestowed upon them. In it is also an instruction for his family and followers regarding the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, so that they may be mindful of Him in all circumstances and make their intention sincerely directed to Him.

The clause ﴿Nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾ is a tadhyil (appended conclusion) to the clause ﴿Indeed You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾. That is, You know our states and You know everything. Because it is a tadhyil, the divine name Allah was made explicit in it, so that the tadhyil would stand independently by itself, in the position of a proverb and a comprehensive statement.

Praise be to God, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Isḥaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication. ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي وهَبَ لِي عَلى الكِبَرِ إسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ إنَّ رَبِّي لِسَمِيعُ الدُّعاءِ﴾ When he (Abraham) asked God for what mattered most to him, namely the establishment of monotheism (tawhid), and hoped that his supplication would be answered, and since that is no marvel in the matter of God, there came to his mind the blessing of God upon him in what he had asked for, namely that He granted him two sons in the prime of old age and at the time when despair of childbirth had set in. So he conversed intimately with God, praised Him for that, and extolled Him by describing Him as "Hearer of supplication," meaning "Responder," that is, one who is characterized by responding as an essential attribute, as a preparation for answering this supplication of his, just as He had answered his earlier supplication. This is the reason for the appropriateness of the placement of this sentence after what precedes it, by the indication of His saying ﴿إنَّ رَبِّي لَسَمِيعُ الدُّعاءِ﴾.

The relative pronoun (al-ism al-mawsul) ﴿الَّذِي﴾ is an allusion to the basis on which praise is built. The (ʿalā) in His saying ʿalā al-kibar (in old age) is for figurative elevation (al-istiʿlaʾ al-majazi), with the meaning of (maʿa, "with"), that is: He granted that in a state elevated above the condition which by its nature does not permit it. For this reason the commentators interpret (ʿalā) here as meaning (maʿa), that is: with old age, in which childbirth does not normally occur. Abraham's age when Isma'il was born to him, peace be upon them both, was eighty-six years (86), and his age when Isḥaq was born to him, peace be upon them both, was one hundred years (100), and no child had been born to him before that. The clause ﴿إنَّ رَبِّي لَسَمِيعُ الدُّعاءِ﴾ is a causal justification (ta'lil) for the clause "who granted" (wahaba), that is: He granted that because He is Hearer of supplication. The Hearer (al-Sami') is used metaphorically (kinayatan) for answering the request, and it is expressed in the form of an intensive (mithal al-mubalagha) or the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha), to indicate the abundance of that and that it is His characteristic, so it conveys that it is an essential attribute of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 40–41:

﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [many] from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day the Reckoning is established.﴾

This is a resumed sentence forming part of his supplication. The verb "make me" (ij'alni) is used in the sense of bringing into being (al-takwin), as was mentioned earlier; that is, "make me, in the future, one who establishes prayer."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 42–43:

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly,﴾ ﴿hastening forward, heads raised, their glance not returning to them, and their hearts empty.﴾

It is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon the preceding sentences, and it is connected to the statement ﴿Say: Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire﴾ [Ibrahim: 30], which is a threat to the polytheists and a warning to them not to be deceived by their safety and security. It is a reminder to them that this is a small, passing enjoyment. So this verse reinforces that threat, together with the incidental consolation of the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what they boast of in terms of blessing and ease, as indicated by the consequential particle in His words ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. Its meaning is also found in His words ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury, and give them respite for a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

Because of the added meaning of consolation and the description of the terrible state of the polytheists on the Day of Gathering that is joined to it, the attaching of this sentence with the conjunction is good, and it was not separated.

The form "lā taḥsabanna" (do not think) apparently is a prohibition against supposing that, but this prohibition is a metaphor (kināya) for affirming and establishing the opposite of what is forbidden, in a context where it would naturally arouse in people the supposition that the forbidden thing occurs, because of the strength of the causes that provoke that. Their being granted respite and the delay of their punishment resembles the state of one who is heedless of their deeds. That is: be certain that Allah is not heedless. This is a second metaphor for the necessary consequence of not being heedless, which is the taking to account. So it is a metaphor with two levels. That is because the prohibition against something indicates that the forbidden thing is such that the addressee might be afflicted with it; thus his prohibition from it is a warning against being afflicted with it, regardless of assuming that the addressee is actually afflicted with that supposition. This usage is the one by which the verse came, whether we make the address to everyone who can be addressed, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in it, or we make it addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) first, and his community is included in it.

The negation of heedlessness from Allah does not proceed according to its literal meaning, because a believer would not suppose that. Rather, it is a metaphor for the prohibition against hastening the punishment of the wrongdoers, and from this came the meaning of consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ).

Ghafla (heedlessness) is ludhūl (distraction, oblivion). It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿And indeed We were unaware of their studying﴾ [al-An'am: 156] in Surat al-An'am.

The intended meaning of ẓulm (wrongdoing) here is shirk (polytheism), because it is wronging oneself by exposing oneself to the cause of painful punishment, and wronging Allah by transgressing against what is due to Him of acknowledging His oneness. It also includes wrongdoing other than shirk, such as wronging people by transgressing against them or depriving them of their rights, for Allah is not unaware of that. For this reason Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: it is a consolation to the wronged and a threat to the wrongdoer.

His words ﴿in which eyes will stare fixedly﴾ explain the sentence ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware...﴾, etc.

Shukhūṣ al-baṣar (the staring of the eye) is its lifting up, like the gaze of one who is stunned and fearful.

The "al-" in al-abṣār (the eyes) is for generality, that is: the eyes of people will stare fixedly from the terror of what they see, and among that is witnessing the terrible states of the wrongdoers.

Al-ihṭāʿ (iḥṭāʿ) is hastening in walking with the neck extended, like one who is cringing, and it is the posture of the fearful.

Iqnāʿ al-ra's (lowering the head) is bowing it from humiliation; it is derived from qana'a, of the pattern manaʿa, when one humbles oneself. ﴿Muhṭiʿīna muqniʿī ruʾūsihim﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl).

The clause ﴿their glance does not return to them﴾ is also in the position of a circumstantial clause. Ṭarf is the movement of the eyelid of the eye.

The meaning of ﴿does not return to them﴾ is: does not come back to them, that is, does not return to its customary state; that is, they cannot turn it. It is a metaphor for the terror of what they have witnessed, to the extent that they remain staring and their eyes do not blink.

His words ﴿and their hearts are empty (hawāʾ)﴾ are an eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh), since they are like air in being devoid of perception because of the intensity of the terror. Hawāʾ in the speech of the Arabs means emptiness (khalāʾ), and it is not the meaning established in the science of medicine or the science of cosmology.
