Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verses 44–45:

﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us for a brief term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers."﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], meaning: console yourself regarding them, do not grow weary of their call, and warn them.

And "mankind" (al-nas) is general, encompassing all of humanity, but the intended meaning is the disbelievers, by the indication of His saying ﴿on the Day the punishment comes to them, when those who did wrong will say﴾. It is also permissible to take "mankind" as a specific known group, namely the polytheists.

﴿The Day the punishment comes to them﴾ is in the accusative as the second object of "warn" (anzir). It is annexed to the clause that follows. The verb of warning (al-indhar) may take a second object by extension (tawassuʿ), since it is construed with the sense of cautioning (tahdhir), as in the hadith: "There was no prophet but that he warned his people of the Dajjal." The phrase "the punishment comes" is used in the sense of its occurrence, as a metonymy by association (majaz mursal).

As for "the punishment" (al-ʿadhab), it is the punishment of the Hereafter, or the punishment of this world with which the polytheists were threatened; and "those who did wrong" are the polytheists.

Page 248
As for the request for the punishment to be delayed: if it is meant as the punishment of the Hereafter, then "delay" means delaying the reckoning, i.e., those who did wrong will say: "Send us back to the world so that we may answer Your call." This is like His saying ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99] ﴿so that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. Thus "delay" is used for returning to the life of this world, as a metonymy by association of the first (majaz mursal bi-ʿalaqat al-awwal). "The messengers" means all the messengers who came to them with the call of Allah.

If it is taken as the punishment of this world, the meaning is that the polytheists say this when they see the onset of punishment upon them; so "delay" here is literal, and "the messengers" in this interpretation is used in the singular sense as a metaphor, referring to Muhammad ﷺ.

"Qarib" (near) means brief in duration; time is likened to distance, meaning: delay us for the amount of time with which we may answer Your call.

* * *

﴿Did you not swear before that there would be no decline for you?﴾ ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth parables for you.﴾

Since the request of those who did wrong from their Lord was mentioned before this clause, it is necessarily understood that the speech following it contains the answer to their request. It is therefore introduced by an implied verb of saying, i.e., it is said to them. The answer was turned away from direct acceptance or rejection toward rebuke and reproach, because that implies the refusal of what they asked. The clause of the answer is opened with the conjunction waw, as an indication of an implied preceding conjoined element, namely the rejection of what they asked, which is omitted for brevity, since it is the nature of one deserving rebuke not to be granted his request. The estimated sense is: "No! Did you not swear...", etc.

"Zawal" (decline) is movement from a place, and it is intended here as departure from the graves toward the reckoning.

Page 249
The object of "zawal" is omitted because the intended meaning is evident, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And they swore by Allah with their strongest oaths that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38].

The clause ﴿You have no decline﴾ explains the clause "you swore." It is not governed by an implied verb of saying; for this reason the first-person pronoun form was not observed in it, so it does not say "we have no decline," but rather the second-person pronoun appropriate to His saying "did you not."

This oath may have been issued by all the wrongdoers while they were in the world, since they received one uniform teaching in polytheism, passed down from predecessors to successors. It is also possible that it was issued by most or some of these nations, while the rest held its meaning implicitly.

Likewise the address in His saying ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ is general to all nations of polytheism except the first of them, and this is a case of restricting generality by reason, since the first nation of polytheists necessarily did not dwell in the dwellings of polytheists.

"Sukna" (dwelling) means residing, and for this reason it is construed with the locative particle, contrary to the original form of the verb, which is transitive by itself. The Arabs used to pass by the dwellings of Thamud on their journey to Syria and would halt there, and they would pass by the dwellings of ʿAd on their journey to Yemen. The clarity of what Allah did to them of punishment is achieved through witnessing the traces of the punishment: sinking into the earth, total annihilation, and the setting forth of parables through words of admonition upon the tongues of the messengers, peace be upon them, and the description of hidden states. He combined for them, in establishing the proof, the evidence of traces and direct witnessing with the evidence of admonition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 46:

[Page 250]
﴿And they had already plotted their plot, but with Allah is their plot, though their plot would have moved mountains from their places.﴾ It may be a conjunction of one report with another report, and it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the people" in His saying ﴿And warn the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 44], meaning: warn them while their plotting is taking place.

Al-makr (plotting): devising and concealing an evil act against another. It has been discussed in His saying ﴿And they plotted, and Allah plotted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54] in Surat Al 'Imran, and in His saying ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 99] in Surat Al-A'raf.

The first "makrahum" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb "makaru", to specify the type, meaning: the kind of plotting for which they were known. The idafa of "makr" to the pronoun "hum" is an idafa of the verbal noun to its agent. Likewise the idafa of the second "makr" to the pronoun "hum".

The "indiyya" (with-ness) is either the with-ness of knowledge, meaning: their plotting is within Allah's knowledge, which is an implicit threat and warning of being held accountable for the evil of their deeds; or the with-ness of creation (takwin), what is called "the plotting of Allah", and its estimation is within Allah's will, so it is a warning of recompense for their plotting.

Al-Jumhur read "li-tazula" with a kasra on the lam and the following present verb in the subjunctive, so "in" is negative and the lam of "li-tazula" is the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), meaning: their plotting was not such that the mountains would be moved by it. This is a belittling of them, meaning: their plotting does not exceed the plotting of their likes, and it is not the kind by which the mountains would be moved. In this there is an allusion that the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, against whom the polytheists intend plotting, will not be shaken by their plotting, for they are like the firm mountains.

Al-Kisa'i alone read "li-tazula" with a fatha on the first lam and a raf' on the second lam, so that "in" is the lightened form of the emphatic "inna", and its governance has been completed, and the lam is the distinguishing lam between it and the negative. The sentence then is an affirmation of the mountains' being moved by their plotting, meaning: it is a great plotting by which the mountains would be moved, had they been capable of moving, i.e., fit for it. So it is used in the sense of fitness and readiness for moving had they been moving. This is from the exaggeration in the occurrence of a matter that is shocking or severe in its kind, like His saying ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 47:

﴿So do not think that Allah would break His promise to His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of Retribution.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') drawn from everything that preceded His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42]. This is the place of consolation (tasliyah), and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is a clear reading of Ibn 'Ashur's wording: "Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 14, verse 52:"

This is the Qur'an, verse 52: "This is a message for the people, so that they may be warned by it, and so that they may know that He is but one God, and so that those of understanding may be reminded." The reference to what precedes it: the pointing (ishara) is to the preceding discourse in the whole surah, from wherever you begin it; you have hit the intended meaning of the pointing, and it is better that it refers to the whole surah.

Al-balagh (the message, conveyance) is the verbal noun of al-tabligh (conveying): that is, this amount of the Qur'an in this surah is a conveying to all the people.

The lam in "li-l-nas" (for the people) is the one known as lam al-tabligh (the lam of communication, indicating the addressee of a statement or something similar to it), which enters upon the name of one who hears a statement or what is similar in meaning.

The conjunction of "wa-li-yunzaru" (and so that they may be warned) to "balagh" is a conjunction to an implied clause that the word balagh indicates, since there is nothing in the sentence before it that is suitable to be conjoined to it. The presence of the lam of the genitive together with the conjunctive waw prevents making it a conjunction to the predicate, because when a prepositional phrase falls as a predicate of the subject, it attaches to it directly without conjunction, as it is in the sense of "existing" or "situated". Predicates are conjoined only when they are descriptions. The implied meaning is: "This is a message for the people so that they may awaken from their heedlessness and so that they may be warned by it."

The lam in "wa-li-yunzaru" is the lam of purpose (kay). A close arrangement of this verse has already been mentioned in His words, "And this is a Book which We have revealed, blessed, confirming that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it" (Al-An'am 92), in Surat al-An'am.

[Page 255]
The meaning: "and so that they may know, from what has been mentioned in it of proofs, that Allah is but one God", that is, restricted to the unique divinity. This is a restriction (qasr) limited to an attribute, and it is relative (idafi), meaning that He, exalted is He, does not exceed that attribute to the attribute of plurality by multiplicity or by trinity, as in His words, "Allah is but one God; glory be to Him that He should have a son" (An-Nisa' 171).

Al-tadhakkur (reminding oneself) is looking into the proofs of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the obligation of following him. For this reason it is specified to "those of understanding", treating others as those who have no intellects: "They are not but like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way" (Al-Furqan 44).

The attributes of the verses referred to by the demonstrative have been ordered in a rational sequence according to the occurrence of some of them after others. It begins with the general attribute, which is the occurrence of the conveying; then what follows the conveying of warning; then what arises from it of knowledge of the oneness, due to the proofs in the course of this surah; then with reminding through what that message has brought, which is the details of knowledge and action. These stages are the comprehensive wisdom of what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, distributed among those to whom it was conveyed. The Muslims are particularly addressed by the meaning of His words, "and so that those of understanding may be reminded."

Surat al-Hijr

This surah is named al-Hijr, and no other name is known for it. The reason for the naming is that the name al-Hijr is not mentioned in any other surah.

Al-Hijr is the name of the land known by it, which is the Hijr of Thamud, and Thamud are the People of al-Hijr. The discussion of it will come at His words, "And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers" (Al-Hijr 80). The Qur'an teachers (al-muktibun) in the kuttab (Qur'anic schools) of Tunisia call it "Surat Rubama", because the word "rubama" (perhaps) occurs in the whole Qur'an only at the beginning of this surah.

It is entirely Meccan, and consensus on this has been reported.

From al-Hasan, the exception of His words, "And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an" (Al-Hijr 87), on the basis that "seven of the oft-repeated" is Surat al-Fatiha and that it is Medinan. This does not hold, because the more correct view is that al-Fatiha is Meccan.

The exception of His words, "As We sent down upon the dividers (al-muqtasimin)" (Al-Hijr 90), "who have made the Qur'an into parts" (Al-Hijr 91), is based on interpreting "al-muqtasimin" as the People of the Book, which is correct. The interpretation of "made the Qur'an into parts" is that they said: "What agrees with our Book is true, and what contradicts our Book is false." Only the Jews of Medina said this. We do not accept this, as we will clarify when discussing that verse.

[Page 6]
Even if this interpretation is granted from both its sides, it is possible, because the Jews heard the Qur'an shortly before the Hijra of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said that at that time. Moreover, it has been narrated that when the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerned Quraysh, they consulted the Jews of Medina about his affair.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Itqan (in 'Ulum al-Qur'an): It is appropriate to except His words, "And We certainly know those who precede among you and We certainly know the late-comers" (Al-Hijr 24), due to what al-Tirmidhi and others narrated about the cause of its revelation, that it concerned the rows of prayer. End of quotation.

He points by that to what al-Tirmidhi narrated through the chain of Nuh ibn Qays al-Judhami, from Abu al-Jawza', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There was a beautiful woman who prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of the people would move forward until they were in the first row so as not to see her, and some would hold back until they were in the last row, that is, of the men's rows. When he bowed, he looked from beneath his armpits." So Allah revealed, "And We certainly know those who precede among you and We certainly know the late-comers" (Al-Hijr 24). Al-Tirmidhi said: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated it without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas, and this is more likely to be more correct than the hadith of Nuh. End of quotation. This is a weakening of the chain of Nuh.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: This hadith contains severe strangeness, and the apparent view is that it is only a statement of Abu al-Jawza' with no mention of Ibn 'Abbas in it. So there is no reliance except on the hadith of Ja'far ibn Sulayman, and it is mursal (disconnected).

On the correction that it is Meccan, it is counted as the fifty-fourth in the count of the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat Yusuf and before Surat al-An'am.

It is strange that they differ about the time of the revelation of this surah, while it contains the verse, "So declare what you are commanded" (Al-Hijr 94). It was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) came out of Dar al-Arqam at the end of the fourth year of his mission.

The number of its verses is ninety-nine by the agreement of the counters.

[Page 7]
The aims of this surah.
It opens with the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a), in which there is an allusion to the challenge with the inimitability of the Qur'an. It emphasizes the excellence of the Qur'an and its guidance, warns the polytheists of a regret they will feel for not having embraced Islam, rebukes them that their immersion in their desires has distracted them from guidance, warns them of destruction when the appointed time of the threat that Allah determined in His knowledge arrives, and consoles the Messenger (ﷺ) for the non-belief of those who have not believed, and for what they say about him and what they demand from him in mockery. It shows that this is the custom of the deniers with their messengers, that signs and warnings are of no benefit to them even if they were given signs according to their demands, and that Allah is the guardian of His Book from their plot. Then it establishes the proof against them by the magnificent work of Allah and the blessings in it upon them, mentions the Resurrection and the evidences of its possibility, and moves to the creation of the human species and what Allah honored this species with, and the story of the disbelief of Satan.

Then it mentions the story of Abraham and Lot, peace be upon them both, the People of the Thicket (al-Ayka), and the People of al-Hijr.

It concludes with the strengthening of the Messenger (ﷺ) and awaiting the hour of victory, that he should pardon those who harm him, leave their affair to Allah, and occupy himself with the believers, and that Allah suffices him against his enemies.

Along with that, there are digressions and insertions, including mention of the creation of the jinn, their eavesdropping on the hearing, the description of the states of the God-fearing, encouragement toward forgiveness, and warning against punishment.
